## Orchestrator-worker pattern

Anthropic's production Research system uses a **lead agent (LeadResearcher)** that plans, then spawns specialized subagents to explore different aspects in parallel [1]. The lead agent analyzes the query, saves its plan to Memory (important because context truncates at 200,000 tokens), and delegates specific research tasks to each subagent [1]. Subagents operate independently—each has its own context window, tools, and search trajectory—then return compressed findings to the lead agent, which synthesizes results and decides whether further research is needed [1].

A **CitationAgent** runs as a final step, processing findings and research reports to attach precise source attributions before results are returned to the user [1].

### When multi-agent systems outperform single agents

A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by **90.2%** on Anthropic's internal research eval [1]. In BrowseComp benchmarking, three factors explained 95% of performance variance: token usage alone explained 80%, with tool-call count and model choice as the other two factors [1].

Token economics matter: agents use ~4× more tokens than chat interactions; multi-agent systems use ~15× more than chats [1]. This makes multi-agent approaches economically viable only for tasks where value justifies the cost. Tasks with high parallelizability, information exceeding single context windows, and many complex tools are the best fit; most coding tasks are a poor fit because they involve fewer truly parallelizable subtasks [1].

### Parallel execution and speed

Two layers of parallelization cut complex research time by up to **90%**: (1) the lead agent spins up 3–5 subagents in parallel (not serially); (2) subagents use 3+ tools in parallel [2].

Currently, the lead agent executes subagent batches synchronously—it waits for each set to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks: the lead cannot steer in-flight subagents, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the system blocks on the slowest subagent [3]. Asynchronous execution would add parallelism but introduces challenges in result coordination, state consistency, and error propagation [3].

### Subagent output and the "game of telephone"

Rather than routing all subagent output through the coordinator, specialized agents write results to external artifact systems (filesystem, external stores) and pass lightweight references back to the lead [4]. This prevents information loss during multi-stage processing and reduces token overhead from copying large outputs through conversation history. It works especially well for structured outputs: code, reports, data visualizations [4].

## Context compression and long-horizon management

As conversations extend beyond standard context windows, agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks [4]. When context limits approach, agents can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts and maintain continuity through careful handoffs; stored context (e.g., the research plan) is retrieved from memory rather than lost [4].

## Production reliability

### Stateful errors and checkpointing

Agents maintain state across many tool calls; errors compound rather than isolate [3]. Restarts from the beginning are expensive and frustrating, so production systems must resume from the point of failure. Anthropic combines AI adaptability (informing the agent when a tool is failing, letting it adapt) with deterministic safeguards: retry logic and regular checkpoints [3].

### Deployment: rainbow deploys

Agent systems run nearly continuously. Code changes must not break agents mid-execution. Anthropic uses **rainbow deployments**—gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously—to avoid disrupting agents at any point in their process [3].

### Tracing and observability

Full production tracing lets teams diagnose why agents failed systematically rather than guessing (bad search queries? poor source selection? tool failure?) [3]. Observability covers agent decision patterns and interaction structures without monitoring individual conversation contents [3].

The OpenAI Agents SDK (TypeScript) provides **traces and spans** that make tools, handoffs, and research steps inspectable and attributable to specific execution points [5]. A trace does not prove correctness and payloads may contain sensitive data; cloud export should not be enabled automatically [5].

## Evaluation

### Start small immediately

Begin with ~20 queries representing real usage patterns; effect sizes in early development are large enough (e.g., 30% → 80% success rate from a single prompt tweak) that small sample sets reveal meaningful signal [6]. Do not wait for large eval suites of hundreds of cases [6].

### LLM-as-judge

LLM judges scale evaluation of free-form research outputs. Anthropic's rubric covers: factual accuracy (claims vs. sources), citation accuracy, completeness, source quality (primary vs. secondary), and tool efficiency [6]. A single LLM call outputting scores 0.0–1.0 plus pass/fail was more consistent than multiple judges evaluating separate components [6]. Works especially well when test cases have a clear answer to check against [6].

### End-state evaluation for stateful agents

For agents that mutate state across many turns, evaluate the final state rather than the intermediate process—agents may reach the same correct outcome via different valid paths [4]. For complex workflows, use discrete checkpoints where specific state changes should have occurred, rather than validating every intermediate step [4].

### Human evaluation

Human testers catch what automated evals miss: hallucinated answers on unusual queries, system failures, subtle source-selection biases. Example: early agents consistently chose SEO-optimized content farms over authoritative academic PDFs or personal blogs—discovered by human testers, fixed by adding source-quality heuristics to prompts [6].

## OpenAI Agents SDK: sessions, handoffs, and tracing

**Sessions** (C01): The SDK provides a `Session` interface with memory and server-backed implementations. `MemorySession` is not durable storage; server-backed sessions are required for persistence across process restarts [7].

**Handoffs** (C02): A handoff transfers control to a specialist agent (with optional input filters controlling what data passes). Using an agent-as-tool keeps the specialist subordinate rather than transferring control. Guardrails do not run universally at every transfer. Handoffs operate within a single SDK run, not as a native protocol between different model providers [8].

## Google ADK MemoryService

The Google Agent Development Kit distinguishes **session state** (scoped to a single conversation) from **MemoryService** (searchable long-term memory across sessions) [9]. Memory can be populated via full session ingestion, event deltas, or explicit entries depending on the backend's capabilities. The in-memory backend loses data on restart; durable backends require explicit configuration. MemoryService is not Orbit's internal memory model [9].

## LangGraph persistence

LangGraph uses **thread-scoped checkpointers** (checkpointing state within a single mission thread) and **cross-thread stores** (shared memory accessible across missions) as distinct primitives [10]. `InMemory` implementations are not durable. This is an optional framework pattern; no migration of Orbit is required [10].

## ReAct reasoning loop

The ReAct pattern (Yao et al., 2023) interleaves reasoning traces and tool actions so that observations from each tool call can correct the next step of the research plan [11]. This makes plan revision after external observations a first-class capability rather than an afterthought. Historical benchmarks used to validate ReAct do not establish present-day reliability guarantees for production systems [11].

spans.quote:
The essence of search is compression: distilling insights from a vast corpus. Subagents facilitate compression by operating in parallel with their own context windows, exploring different aspects of the question simultaneously before condensing the most important tokens for the lead research agent. Each subagent also provides separation of concerns—distinct tools, prompts, and exploration trajectories—which reduces path dependency and enables thorough, independent investigations.

Once intelligence reaches a threshold, multi-agent systems become a vital way to scale performance. For instance, although individual humans have become more intelligent in the last 100,000 years, human societies have become _exponentially_ more capable in the information age because of our _collective_ intelligence and ability to coordinate. Even generally-intelligent agents face limits when operating as individuals; groups of agents can accomplish far more.

Our internal evaluations show that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. We found that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval. For example, when asked to identify all the board members of the companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found the correct answers by decomposing this into tasks for subagents, while the single agent system failed to find the answer with slow, sequential searches.

Multi-agent systems work mainly because they help spend enough tokens to solve the problem. In our analysis, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance in the [BrowseComp](https://openai.com/index/browsecomp/) evaluation (which tests the ability of browsing agents to locate hard-to-find information). We found that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and the model choice as the two other explanatory factors. This finding validates our architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning. The latest Claude models act as large efficiency multipliers on token use, as upgrading to Claude Sonnet 4 is a larger performance gain than doubling the token budget on Claude Sonnet 3.7. Multi-agent architectures effectively scale token usage for tasks that exceed the limits of single agents.

There is a downside: in practice, these architectures burn through tokens fast. In our data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. For economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance. Further, some domains that require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today. For instance, most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research, and LLM agents are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time. We’ve found that multi-agent systems excel at valuable tasks that involve heavy parallelization, information that exceeds single context windows, and interfacing with numerous complex tools.


### Architecture overview for Research

Our Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel.

![](https://www.anthropic.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F1198befc0b33726c45692ac40f764022f4de1bf2-4584x2579.png&w=3840&q=75)The multi-agent architecture in action: user queries flow through a lead agent that creates specialized subagents to search for different aspects in parallel.

When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. As shown in the diagram above, the subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information, in this case on AI agent companies in 2025, and then returning a list of companies to the lead agent so it can compile a final answer.

Traditional approaches using Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) use static retrieval. That is, they fetch some set of chunks that are most similar to an input query and use these chunks to generate a response. In contrast, our architecture uses a multi-step search that dynamically finds relevant information, adapts to new findings, and analyzes results to formulate high-quality answers.

![](https://www.anthropic.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F3bde53c9578d74f6e05c3e515e20b910c5a8c20a-4584x4584.png&w=3840&q=75)Process diagram showing the complete workflow of our multi-agent Research system. When a user submits a query, the system creates a LeadResearcher agent that enters an iterative research process. The LeadResearcher begins by thinking through the approach and saving its plan to Memory to persist the context, since if the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens it will be truncated and it is important to retain the plan. It then creates specialized Subagents (two are shown here, but it can be any number) with specific research tasks. Each Subagent independently performs web searches, evaluates tool results using [interleaved thinking](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/extended-thinking#interleaved-thinking), and returns findings to the LeadResearcher. The LeadResearcher synthesizes these results and decides whether more research is needed—if so, it can create additional subagents or refine its strategy. Once sufficient information is gathered, the system exits the research loop and passes all findings to a CitationAgent, which processes the documents and research report to identify specific locations for citations. This ensures all claims are properly attributed to their sources. The final research results, complete with citations, are then returned to the user.

citations.supports: Orchestrator-worker architecture, LeadResearcher/subagent pattern, CitationAgent, context truncation at 200k tokens, 90.2% performance gain, BrowseComp 95%/80% variance factors, token usage ratios (4x/15x), parallelization bottleneck, synchronous vs async tradeoffs

spans.quote: 2. **Teach the orchestrator how to delegate.** In our system, the lead agent decomposes queries into subtasks and describes them to subagents. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information. We started by allowing the lead agent to give simple, short instructions like 'research the semiconductor shortage,' but found these instructions often were vague enough that subagents misinterpreted the task or performed the exact same searches as other agents. For instance, one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while 2 others duplicated work investigating current 2025 supply chains, without an effective division of labor.

citations.supports: Parallel tool calling cutting research time by up to 90%; 3-5 subagents in parallel; subagents using 3+ tools in parallel; effort scaling rules; prompt engineering principles

spans.quote:
## Appendix

Below are some additional miscellaneous tips for multi-agent systems.

**End-state evaluation of agents that mutate state over many turns.** Evaluating agents that modify persistent state across multi-turn conversations presents unique challenges. Unlike read-only research tasks, each action can change the environment for subsequent steps, creating dependencies that traditional evaluation methods struggle to handle. We found success focusing on end-state evaluation rather than turn-by-turn analysis. Instead of judging whether the agent followed a specific process, evaluate whether it achieved the correct final state. This approach acknowledges that agents may find alternative paths to the same goal while still ensuring they deliver the intended outcome. For complex workflows, break evaluation into discrete checkpoints where specific state changes should have occurred, rather than attempting to validate every intermediate step.

**Long-horizon conversation management.** Production agents often engage in conversations spanning hundreds of turns, requiring careful context management strategies. As conversations extend, standard context windows become insufficient, necessitating intelligent compression and memory mechanisms. We implemented patterns where agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. When context limits approach, agents can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs. Further, they can retrieve stored context like the research plan from their memory rather than losing previous work when reaching the context limit. This distributed approach prevents context overflow while preserving conversation coherence across extended interactions.

**Subagent output to a filesystem to minimize the ‘game of telephone.’** Direct subagent outputs can bypass the main coordinator for certain types of results, improving both fidelity and performance. Rather than requiring subagents to communicate everything through the lead agent, implement artifact systems where specialized agents can create outputs that persist independently. Subagents call tools to store their work in external systems, then pass lightweight references back to the coordinator. This prevents information loss during multi-stage processing and reduces token overhead from copying large outputs through conversation history. The pattern works particularly well for structured outputs like code, reports, or data visualizations where the subagent's specialized prompt produces better results than filtering through a general coordinator.

citations.supports: End-state evaluation for stateful agents; discrete checkpoints; long-horizon context compression; subagent filesystem artifact pattern to avoid game of telephone

spans.quote:
**Start evaluating immediately with small samples**. In early agent development, changes tend to have dramatic impacts because there is abundant low-hanging fruit. A prompt tweak might boost success rates from 30% to 80%. With effect sizes this large, you can spot changes with just a few test cases. We started with a set of about 20 queries representing real usage patterns. Testing these queries often allowed us to clearly see the impact of changes. We often hear that AI developer teams delay creating evals because they believe that only large evals with hundreds of test cases are useful. However, it’s best to start with small-scale testing right away with a few examples, rather than delaying until you can build more thorough evals.

**LLM-as-judge evaluation scales when done well.** Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically, since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. LLMs are a natural fit for grading outputs. We used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (do claims match sources?), citation accuracy (do the cited sources match the claims?), completeness (are all requested aspects covered?), source quality (did it use primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources?), and tool efficiency (did it use the right tools a reasonable number of times?). We experimented with multiple judges to evaluate each component, but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements. This method was especially effective when the eval test cases _did_ have a clear answer, and we could use the LLM judge to simply check if the answer was correct (i.e. did it accurately list the pharma companies with the top 3 largest R&D budgets?). Using an LLM as a judge allowed us to scalably evaluate hundreds of outputs.

**Human evaluation catches what automation misses.** People testing agents find edge cases that evals miss. These include hallucinated answers on unusual queries, system failures, or subtle source selection biases. In our case, human testers noticed that our early agents consistently chose SEO-optimized content farms over authoritative but less highly-ranked sources like academic PDFs or personal blogs. Adding source quality heuristics to our prompts helped resolve this issue. Even in a world of automated evaluations, manual testing remains essential.

Multi-agent systems have emergent behaviors, which arise without specific programming. For instance, small changes to the lead agent can unpredictably change how subagents behave. Success requires understanding interaction patterns, not just individual agent behavior. Therefore, the best prompts for these agents are not just strict instructions, but frameworks for collaboration that define the division of labor, problem-solving approaches, and effort budgets. Getting this right relies on careful prompting and tool design, solid heuristics, observability, and tight feedback loops.See the [open-source prompts in our Cookbook](https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/patterns-agents-basic-workflows) for example prompts from our system.


### Production reliability and engineering challenges

entries.body:
Four prompting strategies underpin Orbit's research agent reasoning. Each addresses a distinct failure mode in multi-step information work.

## Plan-and-Solve (PS) Prompting

Source: Wang et al. (2023), arXiv 2305.04091 [1].

PS prompting instructs the model to first produce an explicit task plan, then execute it step by step. This targets three specific error classes: missing steps (the agent skips a required subtask), calculation errors (arithmetic performed without structure), and semantic errors (misinterpretation of what a step requires). By separating planning from execution, the approach reduces omitted steps compared to standard zero-shot chain-of-thought. **Limitation:** planning alone does not guarantee source quality or numerical correctness; results were measured on reasoning benchmarks with historical models and require local retesting.

## Self-Ask / Compositionality Gap

Source: Press et al. (2023), ACL Findings EMNLP 2023.378 [2].

Self-ask makes dependent subquestions explicit before synthesis. When a research question requires composing multiple facts, the agent surfaces each sub-question as a named step and allows a search engine (or tool call) to answer each one independently before combining them. This closes the "compositionality gap" — the gap between a model's ability to answer component questions individually versus answering their composition in a single pass. **Limitation:** correct component facts do not guarantee a correct composed answer; findings are GPT-3-era and need local retesting on current models.

## Least-to-Most Prompting (LtM)

Source: Zhou et al. (arXiv 2205.10625, revised 2023-04-16) [3].

LtM separates decomposition from solving. Phase 1: decompose the problem into ordered subproblems. Phase 2: solve them sequentially, carrying each resolved answer forward as context for the next. The key property is dependency ordering — simpler or prerequisite subproblems come first, so later steps can reuse already-established facts rather than re-deriving them. Demonstrated on symbolic, compositional, and mathematical tasks. **Limitation:** transfer to open-web research tasks is untested; benefits in retrieval-heavy settings are an open question.

## Clarifying Question Selection

Source: Aliannejadi et al. (2019), arXiv 1907.06554 [4].

The Qulac framework separates three sub-tasks that are often conflated: (1) question retrieval (what clarifying questions are possible?), (2) question selection (which one is most useful given conversation context?), and (3) document retrieval (answering the selected question). For ambiguous or faceted information needs, selecting the right clarifying question using conversation context improves downstream retrieval. **Limitation:** evaluated on offline TREC-based data with oracle analyses; no headline improvement figure is admitted from the retrieved sections, and the ACM-copyrighted paper's downstream license was not verified during selection.

## Applying These in Orbit Research Agents

| Technique | Primary error addressed | Key mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Plan-and-Solve | Missing steps, semantic errors | Explicit plan before execution |
| Self-Ask | Compositionality gap | Named subquestions + per-question lookup |
| Least-to-Most | Dependency failures | Ordered decomposition + answer carry-forward |
| Clarifying Questions | Ambiguous/faceted queries | Question selection via conversation context |

For multi-agent coordination and task delegation at the architecture level (orchestrator-worker patterns, parallel execution, handoffs), see `agents/architecture`. For prompt injection defenses, see `security/prompt-injection`.

## OpenAI: `o3-deep-research` and `o4-mini-deep-research`

Both models are accessed via the **Responses API** [1]. They can browse and synthesize hundreds of sources to produce analyst-level reports. Use cases: legal/scientific research, market analysis, large internal corpora [1].

**Mandatory tool requirement:** at least one data source must be included — web search (`web_search_preview`), remote MCP server, or file search with vector stores [1]. The code interpreter tool (`code_interpreter`) can be added alongside these for complex analysis [1].

**Background mode** (`background=true`) is strongly recommended because tasks can take tens of minutes [1]. Background mode retains response data for roughly 10 minutes to support polling; this makes it **incompatible with strict Zero Data Retention (ZDR)** — OpenAI still accepts `background=true` on ZDR credentials for legacy reasons but advises leaving it off for ZDR compliance [1]. Modified Abuse Monitoring (MAM) organizations can safely use background mode [1].

### Output structure (Responses API)

The response `output` array contains [1]:

| Item type | Description |
|---|---|
| `web_search_call` | Each call includes an `action` (`search`, `open_page`, `find_in_page`) |
| `code_interpreter_call` | Code execution step |
| `mcp_tool_call` | Remote MCP server call |
| `file_search_call` | File search over vector stores |
| `message` | Final answer with inline citations and annotation metadata |

Citations in the final `message` item include `url`, `title`, `start_index`, and `end_index` fields; inline citations must be displayed as clearly visible, clickable links [1].

### Three-step prompt workflow

The Responses API does **not** include an automatic clarification step; the deep research model receives the prompt as-is and starts immediately [2]. To replicate ChatGPT Deep Research behavior, developers build a three-step pipeline [2]:

1. **Clarification** — a faster model (e.g., `gpt-4.1`) asks follow-up questions to gather preferences and constraints.
2. **Prompt rewriting** — the same intermediate model produces a detailed, expanded prompt from the user input + clarifications.
3. **Deep research** — the enriched prompt is passed to `o3-deep-research` or `o4-mini-deep-research`.

All three steps are optional if the initial prompt is already sufficiently detailed [2].

### Connecting to private data

Four methods for private/internal data [2]:

- **Prompt text** — include data inline (simple but not scalable).
- **Vector stores + file search** — maximum two vector stores at a time; only `type` and `vector_store_ids` parameters are supported [2].
- **Connectors** — third-party integrations (Dropbox, Gmail) exposed as built-in tools via the Responses API.
- **Remote MCP servers** — must implement a `search` tool (takes a query, returns results) and a `fetch` tool (takes an id, returns a document); `require_approval` must be set to `never` [2].

**MCP constraint:** only search-and-fetch-pattern MCP servers are supported; general function calling or arbitrary MCP tools are not. Use `o3` instead when non-search tool calls are required [2].

### Cost control

Use `max_tool_calls` to limit the total number of tool calls (web search, MCP calls, etc.) before the model returns — the primary lever for constraining cost and latency [1].

---

## Gemini Deep Research agent

Gemini's deep research capability is an **agent**, not a model variant; it runs via the **Interactions API** [3][4]. The agent autonomously plans, searches, reads, and synthesizes, producing detailed cited reports. Tasks take minutes rather than seconds [3].

**Available versions:**

| Agent ID | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `deep-research-preview-04-2026` | Speed and efficiency; suited for streaming back to a client UI |
| `deep-research-max-preview-04-2026` | Maximum comprehensiveness for automated gathering and synthesis |

**Background execution required** — `background=True` must be set; `store=True` is also required when using background mode [3][5]. Because `store=True` is required for this agent path, it is **incompatible with zero-data-footprint** (which requires `store=false`) [5].

### Agent configuration (`agent_config`)

Pass `agent_config` with `type: "deep-research"` and the fields below [3]:

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `type` | string | Required | Must be `"deep-research"` |
| `thinking_summaries` | string | `"none"` | `"auto"` streams intermediate reasoning steps |
| `visualization` | string | `"auto"` | `"auto"` enables agent-generated charts/images; `"off"` disables |
| `collaborative_planning` | boolean | `false` | `true` enables multi-turn plan review before research begins |

### Collaborative planning (3-step)

When `collaborative_planning=True`, the agent returns a research plan instead of executing immediately [4]:

1. **Request plan** — create an interaction with `collaborative_planning=True`.
2. **Refine plan (optional)** — use `previous_interaction_id` with `collaborative_planning=True` to iterate.
3. **Approve and execute** — set `collaborative_planning=False` (or omit) and pass `previous_interaction_id` from the refined plan.

### Supported tools

By default (no `tools` parameter), the agent has Google Search, URL Context, and Code Execution enabled [4]:

| Tool | `type` value | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Google Search | `google_search` | Yes |
| URL Context | `url_context` | Yes |
| Code Execution | `code_execution` | Yes |
| MCP Server | `mcp_server` | No |
| File Search | `file_search` | No |

MCP server fields: `type`, `name`, `url`, `headers` (auth tokens), `allowed_tools` [4]. Custom function calling tools are **not** supported; use MCP servers instead [3].

**Limitations:** no structured output support; maximum research time 60 minutes (most tasks complete within 20 minutes); Google Search is enabled by default and specific use restrictions apply to grounded results [3].

### Streaming and reconnection

Stream updates by passing `stream=True`. Track the `last_event_id` from each event; if the connection drops, reconnect via `GET /interactions/{id}?stream=true&last_event_id={last_event_id}` [3].

### Follow-up interactions

After a report completes, continue the conversation using `previous_interaction_id` to ask for clarification or elaboration without restarting research [3].

### Pricing

Pay-as-you-go based on underlying model usage and tools [3]:

| Variant | Typical query profile | Estimated cost per task |
|---|---|---|
| `deep-research-preview-04-2026` | ~80 searches, ~250k input tokens (50–70% cached), ~60k output tokens | ~$1.00–$3.00 |
| `deep-research-max-preview-04-2026` | ~160 searches, ~900k input tokens (50–70% cached), ~80k output tokens | ~$3.00–$7.00 |

### Safety considerations

- **Prompt injection via files:** malicious files can manipulate agent output; only upload documents from trusted sources [3].
- **Web content risks:** the agent accesses the public web; review `citations` in the response to verify sources [3].
- **Exfiltration risk:** be cautious mixing sensitive internal data with web access [3].

When displaying web results or information contained in web results to end
users, inline citations should be made clearly visible and clickable in your
user interface.


### Best practices

Deep research models are agentic and conduct multi-step research. This means that they can take tens of minutes to complete tasks. To improve reliability, we recommend using [background mode](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/background), which allows you to execute long running tasks without worrying about timeouts or connectivity issues. In addition, you can also use [webhooks](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/webhooks) to receive a notification when a response is ready. Background mode can be used with the MCP tool or file search tool and is available for [Modified Abuse Monitoring](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data#modified-abuse-monitoring) organizations.

While we strongly recommend using [background mode](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/background), if you choose to not use it then we recommend setting higher timeouts for requests. The OpenAI SDKs support setting timeouts e.g. in the [Python SDK](https://github.com/openai/openai-python?tab=readme-ov-file#timeouts) or [JavaScript SDK](https://github.com/openai/openai-node?tab=readme-ov-file#timeouts).

You can also use the `max_tool_calls` parameter when creating a deep research request to control the total number of tool calls (like to web search or an MCP server) that the model will make before returning a result. This is the primary tool available to you to constrain cost and latency when using these models.

## Prompting deep research models

If you’ve used Deep Research in ChatGPT, you may have noticed that it asks follow-up questions after you submit a query. Deep Research in ChatGPT follows a three step process:

1. **Clarification**: When you ask a question, an intermediate model (like `gpt-4.1`) helps clarify the user’s intent and gather more context (such as preferences, goals, or constraints) before the research process begins. This extra step helps the system tailor its web searches and return more relevant and targeted results.
2. **Prompt rewriting**: An intermediate model (like `gpt-4.1`) takes the original user input and clarifications, and produces a more detailed prompt.
3. **Deep research**: The detailed, expanded prompt is passed to the deep research model, which conducts research and returns it.

Deep research via the Responses API does not include a clarification or prompt rewriting step. As a developer, you can configure this processing step to rewrite the user prompt or ask a set of clarifying questions, since the model expects fully-formed prompts up front and will not ask for additional context or fill in missing information; it simply starts researching based on the input it receives. These steps are optional: if you have a sufficiently detailed prompt, there’s no need to clarify or rewrite it. Below we include an examples of asking clarifying questions and rewriting the prompt before passing it to the deep research models.

Asking clarifying questions using a faster, smaller model

import OpenAI from "openai";
const openai = new OpenAI();

Deep research models are designed to access both public and private data sources, but they require a specific setup for private or internal data. By default, these models can access information on the public internet via the [web search tool](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-web-search). To give the model access to your own data, you have several options:

- Include relevant data directly in the prompt text
- Upload files to vector stores, and use the file search tool to connect model to vector stores
- Use [connectors](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-remote-mcp#connectors) to pull in context from popular applications, like Dropbox and Gmail
- Connect the model to a remote MCP server that can access your data source


### Prompt text

Though perhaps the most straightforward, it’s not the most efficient or scalable way to perform deep research with your own data. See other techniques below.


### Vector stores

In most cases, you’ll want to use the file search tool connected to vector stores that you manage. Deep research models only support the required parameters for the file search tool, namely `type` and `vector_store_ids`. You can attach multiple vector stores at a time, with a current maximum of two vector stores.


### Connectors

Connectors are third-party integrations with popular applications, like Dropbox and Gmail, that let you pull in context to build richer experiences in a single API call. In the Responses API, you can think of these connectors as built-in tools, with a third-party backend. Learn how to [set up connectors](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-remote-mcp#connectors) in the remote MCP guide.


### Remote MCP servers

If you need to use a remote MCP server instead, deep research models require a specialized type of MCP server—one that implements a search and fetch interface. The model is optimized to call data sources exposed through this interface and doesn’t support tool calls or MCP servers that don’t implement this interface. If supporting other types of tool calls and MCP servers is important to you, we recommend using the generic o3 model with MCP or function calling instead. o3 is also capable of performing multi-step research tasks with some guidance to do so in its prompts.

To integrate with a deep research model, your MCP server must provide:

- A `search` tool that takes a query and returns search results.
- A `fetch` tool that takes an id from the search results and returns the corresponding document.

For more details on the required schemas, how to build a compatible MCP server, and an example of a compatible MCP server, see our [deep research MCP guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/mcp).

Lastly, in deep research, the approval mode for MCP tools must have `require_approval` set to `never`—since both the search and fetch actions are read-only the human-in-the-loop reviews add lesser value and are currently unsupported.

The Gemini Developer API Deep Research agent runs as a background interaction. Google's documentation says that background execution requires `store=True`. This is a requirement of this specific agent path, not a claim about every Gemini model invocation.

## Zero-data-footprint condition

Source: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/zdr

Google's Zero Data Retention documentation says that for the Interactions API, `store=false` is required for zero-data footprint. The page also describes separate exceptions and data handling for tools such as Google Search grounding; those must be assessed separately.

## Scope of the comparison

For this Gemini Developer API Deep Research agent path, the documented `store=True` requirement and the documented `store=false` condition for zero-data footprint cannot both hold for the same interaction. Therefore, do not claim that this path meets a strict zero-data-footprint requirement. This comparison does not establish a blanket rule for all Google research products or account agreements. Verify the provider's current terms and the selected tools before asserting retention properties.

For comparison only: OpenAI's Deep Research guide at https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/deep-research states its background mode is incompatible with strict Zero Data Retention because of temporary polling storage. OpenAI's implementation and contractual terms are distinct from Google's; do not treat them as the same underlying policy.

## Safety considerations

Giving an agent access to the web and your private files requires careful
consideration of safety risks.

- **Prompt injection using files:** The agent reads the contents of the files
you provide. Ensure that uploaded documents (PDFs, text files) come from
trusted sources. A malicious file could contain hidden text designed to
manipulate the agent's output.
- **Web content risks:** The agent searches the public web. While we implement
robust safety filters, there is a risk that the agent may encounter and
process malicious web pages. We recommend reviewing the `citations` provided
in the response to verify the sources.
- **Exfiltration:** Be cautious when asking the agent to summarize sensitive
internal data if you are also allowing it to browse the web.


## Best practices

- **Prompt for unknowns:** Instruct the agent on how to handle missing data.
For example, add _"If specific figures for 2025 are not available,_
_explicitly state they are projections or unavailable rather than_
_estimating"_ to your prompt.
- **Provide context:** Ground the agent's research by providing background
information or constraints directly in the input prompt.
- **Use collaborative planning:** For complex queries, enable collaborative
planning to review and refine the research plan before execution.
- **Multimodal inputs:** Deep Research agent supports multi-modal inputs.
Use cautiously, as this increases costs and risks context window overflow.


## Limitations

- **Custom tools:** You cannot currently provide custom Function Calling tools
but you can use remote MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers with the Deep Research agent.
- **Structured output:** The Deep Research agent currently
doesn't support structured outputs.
- **Max research time:** The Deep Research agent has a maximum research time
of 60 minutes. Most tasks should complete within 20 minutes.
- **Store requirement:** Agent execution using `background=True` requires
`store=True`.
- **Google search:** [Google\\
Search](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/google-search) is enabled by
default and [specific\\
restrictions](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms#use-restrictions2)
apply to the grounded results.

multi-step research tasks. Powered by Gemini, it navigates complex
information landscapes to produce detailed, cited reports. New
capabilities allow you to collaboratively plan with the agent, connect to
external tools using MCP servers, include
visualizations (like charts and graphs), and provide documents directly
as input.

The following example shows how to start a research task in the background
and poll for results.

entries.body:
Four complementary frameworks address whether a generated statement is genuinely attributable to its cited sources. Each targets a distinct layer of the attribution problem.

## AIS — Attributable to Identified Sources (Rashkin et al. 2023)

AIS defines a two-stage annotation framework for measuring whether NLG output is attributable to an identified source [1]. The core check is interpretability-then-attribution: a statement must first be interpretable in context before attribution is assessed. Source quality and other output characteristics (e.g., fluency, overall correctness) are deliberately kept as separate dimensions — AIS does not ask whether the source is trustworthy or the claim globally true, only whether the generated text is supported by the provided source [1]. The paper is published under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; commercial use and derivative works require further licence assessment [1].

## ALCE — Separating Fluency, Correctness, and Citation Quality (Gao et al. 2023)

ALCE (Gao, Yen, Yu, Chen; Princeton, EMNLP 2023) benchmarks citation-grounded long-form answer generation and explicitly separates three evaluation dimensions [2]:

- **Fluency** — grammatical and readable prose.
- **Correctness** — factual accuracy of the answer.
- **Citation quality** — whether cited passages actually support the claims they are attached to.

Citation quality is further broken down into *support coverage* (does at least one cited passage entail the statement?) and *irrelevant citation* detection (are passages cited that add no support?) [2]. Multiple passages may jointly support a single statement. Automatic evaluation uses entailment models rather than human annotation, so results are model- and corpus-specific, not ground truth [2].

## MultiAttr and PolitiCite — Post-Generation Multi-Source Citation (Patel et al. 2024)

MultiAttr and PolitiCite (Patel, Subramanian, Garg, Banerjee, Misra; NAACL 2024) address long-form answers that draw on several evidence sources simultaneously [3]. The key distinction from ALCE-style evaluation is the task formulation: citation assignment happens *after* generation (post-generation citation), not jointly during answer generation [3]. The framework assumes retrieved source text is true and that a retriever already exists; it therefore does not establish source quality or retrieval completeness, and results do not validate any production system [3].

## Lost-in-the-Middle — Positional Bias in Long Contexts (Liu et al. 2024)

Liu, Lin, Hewitt et al. (TACL 2024) study multi-document QA and key-value retrieval to measure how evidence position within a long context affects model performance [4]. Language models tend to underuse evidence placed in the middle of a long context — recall is higher for evidence near the beginning or end. This positional bias is relevant when assembling retrieved chunks into a context window: ordering matters, and recall should be tested both before and after context assembly [4]. Results are specific to the models and tasks studied; the paper does not show that all current models fail, nor does it provide a lossless compaction recipe [4].

## Practical Distinctions

| Framework | Stage | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| AIS | Post-generation | Is the statement attributable to the cited source? |
| ALCE | Evaluation benchmark | Separates fluency / correctness / citation support |
| MultiAttr / PolitiCite | Post-generation citation assignment | Multi-source attribution for long-form answers |
| Lost-in-the-Middle | Context assembly | Positional bias; evidence ordering in retrieval |

For operational Ragas metrics (Faithfulness, Context Precision, Context Recall, HHEM-2.1-Open), see `evaluation/rag_metrics/ragas`.

Three core Ragas metrics for RAG evaluation: **Faithfulness**, **Context Recall**, and **Context Precision**. All support both a modern collections-based API and a legacy `SingleTurnSample` API (legacy deprecated in v0.4, removed in v1.0). The recommended LLM for new integrations is `gpt-4o-mini` via `llm_factory`.

## Faithfulness

Measures factual consistency of the generated `response` against `retrieved_contexts`. Scores range 0–1; higher = more consistent [1].

**Calculation (3 steps):**
1. Decompose the response into individual claims.
2. Check each claim against the retrieved context to determine if it can be inferred.
3. Apply the formula:

`Faithfulness Score = (Claims supported by context) / (Total claims in response)` [1]

**Example:** A response making 2 claims where only 1 is supported yields a score of 0.5 [1].

**Collections API (recommended):**
```python
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from ragas.llms import llm_factory
from ragas.metrics.collections import Faithfulness

client = AsyncOpenAI()
llm = llm_factory("gpt-4o-mini", client=client)
scorer = Faithfulness(llm=llm)

result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="When was the first super bowl?",
    response="The first superbowl was held on Jan 15, 1967",
    retrieved_contexts=["The First AFL–NFL World Championship Game was an American football game played on January 15, 1967..."]
)
# result.value → 1.0
```

**Faithfulness with HHEM-2.1-Open:** Vectara's `HHEM-2.1-Open` (T5 classifier) can replace the LLM in step 2 (claim-context inference). It is free, small, and open-source, suitable for production. Use `FaithfulnesswithHHEM` from the legacy API. Supports `device` (default: CPU) and `batch_size` (default: 10) parameters [1]:

```python
from ragas.metrics import FaithfulnesswithHHEM
scorer = FaithfulnesswithHHEM(device="cuda:0", batch_size=10)
await scorer.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

---

## Context Recall

Measures how many relevant documents were successfully retrieved — penalizes missing results. Requires a `reference` answer as a proxy for `reference_contexts` [2].

**Formula:** `Context Recall = (Claims in reference supported by retrieved context) / (Total claims in reference)` [2]

**Three variants:**

| Variant | Class | Inputs | Method |
|---|---|---|---|
| LLM-based | `ContextRecall` | `user_input`, `retrieved_contexts`, `reference` | LLM claim decomposition |
| Non-LLM | `NonLLMContextRecall` | `retrieved_contexts`, `reference_contexts` | String comparison (e.g. Levenshtein) |
| ID-based | `IDBasedContextRecall` | `retrieved_context_ids`, `reference_context_ids` | Set intersection |

**ID-based formula:** `(Reference IDs found in retrieved IDs) / (Total reference IDs)` [2]

**Collections API example (LLM-based):**
```python
from ragas.metrics.collections import ContextRecall
scorer = ContextRecall(llm=llm)
result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    retrieved_contexts=["Paris is the capital of France."],
    reference="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris."
)
# result.value → 1.0
```

**Non-LLM example:** With `retrieved_contexts=["Paris is the capital of France."]` and `reference_contexts=["Paris is the capital of France.", "The Eiffel Tower is one of the most famous landmarks in Paris."]`, score = 0.5 (1 of 2 reference contexts matched) [2].

**ID-based example:** `retrieved_context_ids=["doc_1","doc_2","doc_3"]`, `reference_context_ids=["doc_1","doc_4","doc_5","doc_6"]` → score = 0.25 (1 of 4 reference IDs found) [2].

---

## Context Precision

Evaluates whether the retriever ranks relevant chunks **higher** than irrelevant ones. Calculated as mean precision@k across all retrieved chunks [3].

**Formula:**
- `Context Precision@K = Σ(Precision@k × vk) / (Total relevant items in top K)`
- `Precision@k = true_positives@k / (true_positives@k + false_positives@k)`
- `vk ∈ {0,1}` is the relevance indicator at rank k [3]

**Key behavior:** Ranking matters. An irrelevant chunk at position 2 (with relevant at position 1) leaves score near 1.0; swapping them reduces the score to ~0.5 [3].

**Four variants:**

| Variant | Class | Inputs | Reference needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| LLM with reference | `ContextPrecision` (collections) / `LLMContextPrecisionWithReference` | `user_input`, `retrieved_contexts`, `reference` | Yes |
| LLM without reference | `ContextUtilization` (collections) / `LLMContextPrecisionWithoutReference` | `user_input`, `retrieved_contexts`, `response` | No |
| Non-LLM with reference contexts | `NonLLMContextPrecisionWithReference` | `retrieved_contexts`, `reference_contexts` | reference_contexts (requires `rapidfuzz`) |
| ID-based | `IDBasedContextPrecision` | `retrieved_context_ids`, `reference_context_ids` | reference_context_ids |

**ID-based formula:** `(Retrieved IDs found in reference IDs) / (Total retrieved IDs)` [3]

**ID-based example:** `retrieved_context_ids=["doc_1","doc_2","doc_3","doc_4"]`, `reference_context_ids=["doc_1","doc_4","doc_5","doc_6"]` → score = 0.5 (2 of 4 retrieved IDs matched) [3].

**Collections API example:**
```python
from ragas.metrics.collections import ContextPrecision
scorer = ContextPrecision(llm=llm)
result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    reference="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    retrieved_contexts=["The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.", "The Brandenburg Gate is located in Berlin."]
)
# result.value → 0.9999999999
```

---

## API Notes

- All metrics support both `.ascore()` (async) and `.score()` (sync) in the collections API [1][2][3].
- Legacy `SingleTurnSample` + `single_turn_ascore()` pattern is deprecated as of v0.4 and will be removed in v1.0 [1][3].
- Attribution/citation quality frameworks (AIS, ALCE, MultiAttr) and positional bias research: see `evaluation/rag_metrics/attribution_frameworks`.

## Faithfulness

The **Faithfulness** metric measures how factually consistent a `response` is with the `retrieved context`. It ranges from 0 to 1, with higher scores indicating better consistency.

A response is considered **faithful** if all its claims can be supported by the retrieved context.

To calculate this:
1\. Identify all the claims in the response.
2\. Check each claim to see if it can be inferred from the retrieved context.
3\. Compute the faithfulness score using the formula:

Faithfulness Score=Number of claims in the response supported by the retrieved contextTotal number of claims in the response

### Example

```
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from ragas.llms import llm_factory
from ragas.metrics.collections import Faithfulness

# Setup LLM
client = AsyncOpenAI()
llm = llm_factory("gpt-4o-mini", client=client)

# Create metric
scorer = Faithfulness(llm=llm)

# Evaluate
result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="When was the first super bowl?",
    response="The first superbowl was held on Jan 15, 1967",
    retrieved_contexts=[\
        "The First AFL–NFL World Championship Game was an American football game played on January 15, 1967, at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum in Los Angeles."\
    ]

print(f"Faithfulness Score: {result.value}")
```

Output:

```
Faithfulness Score: 1.0
```

Synchronous Usage

If you prefer synchronous code, you can use the `.score()` method instead of `.ascore()`:

```
result = scorer.score(
    user_input="When was the first super bowl?",
    response="The first superbowl was held on Jan 15, 1967",
    retrieved_contexts=[...]
)
```

### How It’s Calculated

Example

**Question**: Where and when was Einstein born?

**Context**: Albert Einstein (born 14 March 1879) was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely held to be one of the greatest and most influential scientists of all time

**High faithfulness answer**: Einstein was born in Germany on 14th March 1879.

**Low faithfulness answer**: Einstein was born in Germany on 20th March 1879.

Let's examine how faithfulness was calculated using the low faithfulness answer:

- Statements:
    - Statement 1: "Einstein was born in Germany."
    - Statement 2: "Einstein was born on 20th March 1879."
- **Step 2:** For each of the generated statements, verify if it can be inferred from the given context.
  - Statement 1: Yes
  - Statement 2: No
- **Step 3:** Use the formula depicted above to calculate faithfulness.

Faithfulness=12=0.5


## Legacy Metrics API

The following examples use the legacy metrics API pattern. For new projects, we recommend using the collections-based API shown above.

Deprecation Timeline

This API will be deprecated in version 0.4 and removed in version 1.0. Please migrate to the collections-based API shown above.

```
from ragas.dataset_schema import SingleTurnSample
from ragas.metrics import Faithfulness

sample = SingleTurnSample(
        user_input="When was the first super bowl?",
        response="The first superbowl was held on Jan 15, 1967",
        retrieved_contexts=[\
            "The First AFL–NFL World Championship Game was an American football game played on January 15, 1967, at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum in Los Angeles."\
        ]
    )
scorer = Faithfulness(llm=evaluator_llm)
await scorer.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

Output:

```
1.0
```

### Faithfulness with HHEM-2.1-Open

[Vectara's HHEM-2.1-Open](https://vectara.com/blog/hhem-2-1-a-better-hallucination-detection-model/) is a classifier model (T5) that is trained to detect hallucinations from LLM generated text. This model can be used in the second step of calculating faithfulness, i.e. when claims are cross-checked with the given context to determine if it can be inferred from the context. The model is free, small, and open-source, making it very efficient in production use cases.

To use the model to calculate faithfulness:

```

from ragas.dataset_schema import SingleTurnSample
from ragas.metrics import FaithfulnesswithHHEM

sample = SingleTurnSample(
        user_input="When was the first super bowl?",
        response="The first superbowl was held on Jan 15, 1967",
        retrieved_contexts=[\
            "The First AFL–NFL World Championship Game was an American football game played on January 15, 1967, at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum in Los Angeles."\
        ]
    )
scorer = FaithfulnesswithHHEM(llm=evaluator_llm)
await scorer.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

You can load the model onto a specified device by setting the `device` argument and adjust the batch size for inference using the `batch_size` parameter. By default, the model is loaded on the CPU with a batch size of 10:

```
my_device = "cuda:0"
my_batch_size = 10

scorer = FaithfulnesswithHHEM(device=my_device, batch_size=my_batch_size)
await scorer.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

Context Recall measures how many of the relevant documents (or pieces of information) were successfully retrieved. It focuses on not missing important results. Higher recall means fewer relevant documents were left out. In short, recall is about not missing anything important.

Since it is about not missing anything, calculating context recall always requires a reference to compare against. The LLM-based Context Recall metric uses `reference` as a proxy to `reference_contexts`, which makes it easier to use as annotating reference contexts can be very time-consuming. To estimate context recall from the `reference`, the reference is broken down into claims, and each claim is analyzed to determine whether it can be attributed to the retrieved context or not. In an ideal scenario, all claims in the reference answer should be attributable to the retrieved context.

The formula for calculating context recall is as follows:

Context Recall=Number of claims in the reference supported by the retrieved contextTotal number of claims in the reference

```
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from ragas.llms import llm_factory
from ragas.metrics.collections import ContextRecall

# Setup LLM
client = AsyncOpenAI()
llm = llm_factory("gpt-4o-mini", client=client)

# Create metric
scorer = ContextRecall(llm=llm)

# Evaluate
result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    retrieved_contexts=["Paris is the capital of France."],
    reference="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris."
)
print(f"Context Recall Score: {result.value}")
```

Output:

```
Context Recall Score: 1.0

retrieved_contexts=["Paris is the capital of France."],
    reference="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris."
)
```

## LLM Based Context Recall (Legacy API)

Legacy API

The following example uses the legacy metrics API pattern. For new projects, we recommend using the collections-based API shown above. This API will be deprecated in version 0.4 and removed in version 1.0.

```
from ragas.dataset_schema import SingleTurnSample
from ragas.metrics import LLMContextRecall

sample = SingleTurnSample(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    response="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    reference="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    retrieved_contexts=["Paris is the capital of France."],
)

context_recall = LLMContextRecall(llm=evaluator_llm)
await context_recall.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

Output:

```
1.0
```

## Non LLM Based Context Recall

`NonLLMContextRecall` metric is computed using `retrieved_contexts` and `reference_contexts`, and the values range between 0 and 1, with higher values indicating better performance. This metrics uses non-LLM string comparison metrics to identify if a retrieved context is relevant or not. You can use any non LLM based metrics as distance measure to identify if a retrieved context is relevant or not.

The formula for calculating context recall is as follows:

context recall=\|Number of relevant contexts retrieved\|\|Total number of reference contexts\|

### Example

```
from ragas.dataset_schema import SingleTurnSample
from ragas.metrics import NonLLMContextRecall

sample = SingleTurnSample(
    retrieved_contexts=["Paris is the capital of France."],
    reference_contexts=["Paris is the capital of France.", "The Eiffel Tower is one of the most famous landmarks in Paris."]
)

context_recall = NonLLMContextRecall()
await context_recall.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

Output

```
0.5
```

## ID BasedContext Recall

ID Based Context Recall
IDBasedContextRecall provides a direct and efficient way to measure recall by comparing the IDs of retrieved contexts with reference context IDs. This metric is particularly useful when you have a unique ID system for your documents and want to evaluate retrieval performance without comparing the actual content.

The metric computes recall using retrieved\_context\_ids and reference\_context\_ids, with values ranging between 0 and 1. Higher values indicate better performance. It works with both string and integer IDs.

The formula for calculating ID-based context recall is as follows:

ID-Based Context Recall=Number of reference context IDs found in retrieved context IDsTotal number of reference context IDs

### Example

```
from ragas.dataset_schema import SingleTurnSample
from ragas.metrics import IDBasedContextRecall

sample = SingleTurnSample(
    retrieved_context_ids=["doc_1", "doc_2", "doc_3"],
    reference_context_ids=["doc_1", "doc_4", "doc_5", "doc_6"]
)

id_recall = IDBasedContextRecall()
await id_recall.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

Output

```
0.25

Context Precision is a metric that evaluates the retriever's ability to rank relevant chunks higher than irrelevant ones for a given query in the retrieved context. Specifically, it assesses the degree to which relevant chunks in the retrieved context are placed at the top of the ranking.

It is calculated as the mean of the precision@k for each chunk in the context. Precision@k is the ratio of the number of relevant chunks at rank k to the total number of chunks at rank k.

Context Precision@K=∑k=1K(Precision@k×vk)Total number of relevant items in the top K results

Precision@k=true positives@k(true positives@k+false positives@k)

Where K is the total number of chunks in `retrieved_contexts` and vk∈{0,1} is the relevance indicator at rank k.

### Context Precision

The `ContextPrecision` metric evaluates whether retrieved contexts are useful for answering a question by comparing each context against a reference answer. Use this when you have a reference answer available.

```
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from ragas.llms import llm_factory
from ragas.metrics.collections import ContextPrecision

# Setup LLM
client = AsyncOpenAI()
llm = llm_factory("gpt-4o-mini", client=client)

# Create metric
scorer = ContextPrecision(llm=llm)

# Evaluate
result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    reference="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    retrieved_contexts=[\
        "The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",\
        "The Brandenburg Gate is located in Berlin."\
    ]
)
print(f"Context Precision Score: {result.value}")
```

Output:

```
Context Precision Score: 0.9999999999
```

Synchronous Usage

If you prefer synchronous code, you can use the `.score()` method instead of `.ascore()`:

```
result = scorer.score(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    reference="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    retrieved_contexts=[...]

```

### Context Utilization

The `ContextUtilization` metric evaluates whether retrieved contexts are useful by comparing each context against the generated response. Use this when you don't have a reference answer but have the response that was generated.

```
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from ragas.llms import llm_factory
from ragas.metrics.collections import ContextUtilization

# Setup LLM
client = AsyncOpenAI()
llm = llm_factory("gpt-4o-mini", client=client)

# Create metric
scorer = ContextUtilization(llm=llm)

# Evaluate
result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    response="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    retrieved_contexts=[\
        "The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",\
        "The Brandenburg Gate is located in Berlin."\
    ]
)
print(f"Context Utilization Score: {result.value}")
```

Output:

```
Context Utilization Score: 0.9999999999
```

Note that even if an irrelevant chunk is present at the second position in the array, context precision remains the same. However, if this irrelevant chunk is placed at the first position, context precision reduces:

```
result = await scorer.ascore(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    response="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    retrieved_contexts=[\
        "The Brandenburg Gate is located in Berlin.",\

]
)
print(f"Context Utilization Score: {result.value}")
```

Output:

```
Context Utilization Score: 0.49999999995
```

## Legacy Metrics API

The following examples use the legacy metrics API pattern. For new projects, we recommend using the collections-based API shown above.

Deprecation Timeline

This API will be deprecated in version 0.4 and removed in version 1.0. Please migrate to the collections-based API shown above.

### Example with SingleTurnSample

```
from ragas import SingleTurnSample
from ragas.metrics import LLMContextPrecisionWithoutReference

context_precision = LLMContextPrecisionWithoutReference(llm=evaluator_llm)

sample = SingleTurnSample(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    response="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    retrieved_contexts=["The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris."],
)

await context_precision.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

Output:

```
0.9999999999
```

### Context Precision without reference

The `LLMContextPrecisionWithoutReference` metric can be used without the availability of a reference answer. To estimate if the retrieved contexts are relevant, this method uses the LLM to compare each chunk in `retrieved_contexts` with the `response`.

#### Example

```
from ragas import SingleTurnSample
from ragas.metrics import LLMContextPrecisionWithoutReference

context_precision = LLMContextPrecisionWithoutReference(llm=evaluator_llm)

sample = SingleTurnSample(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    response="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    retrieved_contexts=["The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris."],
)

await context_precision.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

Output:

```
0.9999999999
```

### Context Precision with reference

The `LLMContextPrecisionWithReference` metric can be used when you have both retrieved contexts and also a reference response associated with a `user_input`. To estimate if the retrieved contexts are relevant, this method uses the LLM to compare each chunk in `retrieved_contexts` with the `reference`.

#### Example

```
from ragas import SingleTurnSample
from ragas.metrics import LLMContextPrecisionWithReference

context_precision = LLMContextPrecisionWithReference(llm=evaluator_llm)

sample = SingleTurnSample(
    user_input="Where is the Eiffel Tower located?",
    reference="The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris.",
    retrieved_contexts=["The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris."],
)

await context_precision.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

Output:

```
0.9999999999
```

## Non LLM Based Context Precision

This metric uses non-LLM-based methods (such as [Levenshtein distance measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levenshtein_distance)) to determine whether a retrieved context is relevant.

### Context Precision with reference contexts

The `NonLLMContextPrecisionWithReference` metric is designed for scenarios where both retrieved contexts and reference contexts are available for a `user_input`. To determine if a retrieved context is relevant, this method compares each retrieved context or chunk in `retrieved_contexts` with every context in `reference_contexts` using a non-LLM-based similarity measure.

Note that this metric would need the rapidfuzz package to be installed: `pip install rapidfuzz`.

#### Example

```

from ragas import SingleTurnSample
from ragas.metrics import NonLLMContextPrecisionWithReference

context_precision = NonLLMContextPrecisionWithReference()

sample = SingleTurnSample(
    retrieved_contexts=["The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris."],
    reference_contexts=["Paris is the capital of France.", "The Eiffel Tower is one of the most famous landmarks in Paris."]
)

await context_precision.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

Output:

```
0.9999999999
```

## ID Based Context Precision

IDBasedContextPrecision provides a direct and efficient way to measure precision by comparing the IDs of retrieved contexts with reference context IDs. This metric is particularly useful when you have a unique ID system for your documents and want to evaluate retrieval performance without comparing the actual content.

The metric computes precision using retrieved\_context\_ids and reference\_context\_ids, with values ranging between 0 and 1. Higher values indicate better performance. It works with both string and integer IDs.

The formula for calculating ID-based context precision is as follows:

ID-Based Context Precision=Number of retrieved context IDs found in reference context IDsTotal number of retrieved context IDs

### Example

```
from ragas import SingleTurnSample
from ragas.metrics import IDBasedContextPrecision

sample = SingleTurnSample(
    retrieved_context_ids=["doc_1", "doc_2", "doc_3", "doc_4"],
    reference_context_ids=["doc_1", "doc_4", "doc_5", "doc_6"]
)

id_precision = IDBasedContextPrecision()
await id_precision.single_turn_ascore(sample)
```

## Dataset Documentation Frameworks

**Datasheets for Datasets** (Gebru et al., arXiv 1803.09010) proposes a structured questionnaire covering dataset composition, collection process, intended uses, and known limitations — to be completed before a dataset is used in any research pipeline [1]. This is complementary to simply listing sources: a datasheet is declarative, so downstream bias and domain shift still require independent verification.

**FAIR Principles** (Wilkinson et al., *Scientific Data*, 2016-03-15) require that datasets and their metadata are Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable [2]. Key nuances: FAIR applies to both data and metadata, not just raw downloads; FAIR does **not** mean open, accurate, or freely reusable — access conditions and reuse rights must be checked separately. Persistent identifiers are a core FAIR requirement for cataloguing sources.

Both frameworks are complementary: FAIR governs how a dataset is registered and addressable; a Datasheet documents what it actually contains and where it may mislead.

## Scholarly QA Benchmarks

**QASPER** (Dasigi et al., NAACL 2021; AI2/UW) is a dataset of information-seeking questions anchored in NLP research papers [3]. Question writing and answering are separated into two roles; answerers must supply evidence. Answer types span extractive, abstractive, yes/no, and unanswerable — the unanswerable category being critical for systems that must know when a paper does not address a question. Text is derived from LaTeX source, so QASPER performance does not validate PDF extraction pipelines.

**AmbigQA** (Min et al., EMNLP 2020) addresses open-domain questions that admit multiple plausible answers due to underlying ambiguity [4]. Each ambiguous question is paired with rewritten, disambiguated variants and their corresponding answers. This is the benchmark to reference when a research question may carry implicit multiple interpretations that need to be surfaced and resolved before synthesis.

**SciFact** (Wadden et al., EMNLP 2020; UW/AI2) formalizes scientific claim verification: each atomic claim is linked to supporting or refuting biomedical abstracts plus minimal rationale sentences [5]. Three outcomes are possible — supported, refuted, insufficient information. Compound claims must be decomposed before evaluation; SciFact does not assign a global truth label and does not substitute for broader expert review. Scope is primarily biomedical abstracts and single-source verification.

**MultiCite** (Lauscher et al., NAACL 2022) extends citation intent modeling beyond single-sentence, single-label settings [6]. It models multi-sentence citation contexts, multiple simultaneous intent labels per citation, and repeated mentions of the same work in different roles. Annotated corpus is computational-linguistics discourse; intent labels do not imply evidence entailment or scientific validity.

## Multi-Document Synthesis Methods

**Multi-XScience** (Lu et al., EMNLP 2020; Mila) is a benchmark for extreme multi-document summarization: given a query paper's abstract and the abstracts of its cited works, the task is to generate a related-work paragraph [7]. The design forces combination across sources rather than copying from the query introduction. Limitation: reference articles are represented only by their abstracts, not full text; target output is related-work prose, not exhaustive source verification. Dataset was built from historical MAG/arXiv data; current availability should be confirmed.

**STORM** (Shao et al., NAACL 2024) is a pipeline for writing Wikipedia-style articles from scratch using LLMs [8]. It separates three stages: (1) perspective discovery across retrieved sources, (2) simulated, source-grounded question generation from each perspective, (3) outline construction followed by article drafting. Known failure modes identified in the paper itself: source-bias transfer (the article inherits the slant of retrieved documents) and over-association of unrelated facts. Relevant when planning multi-perspective research outlines before drafting.

## Measurement Uncertainty in Evidence

**NIST TN 1297** (Taylor & Kuyatt, 1994) distinguishes Type A uncertainty components (evaluated by statistical analysis of a series of observations) from Type B components (evaluated by other means, e.g., prior data, manufacturer specs, expert judgment) [9]. The standard combined uncertainty combines both. This framework is useful when interpreting quantitative claims in sources: uncertainty is not synonymous with error, and a measurement result should always carry an associated uncertainty statement. Note: the formulas assume physical measurement units with appropriate covariance; they do not directly transfer to LLM confidence scores without careful re-specification.
