A schema describes the types of documents and fields editors may author in a Sanity Studio workspace.

Copy articleCopy article

The top level `schema` configuration accepts an object with two properties: `templates` and `types:`

- The `templates` property accepts an array of Initial Value Template configuration objects or a callback function returning the same.
- The `types` property accepts an array of schema definition objects or a callback function returning the same.

In both cases, the callback function is called with the current value as the first argument and a context object as the second. Thus, you can access schema definitions and Initial Value Templates implemented by plugins.

- ##### [templates](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#templates-3b7c7ccbff27 "Copy link to this section")



array \| function

An array of schema definitions or a callback function that resolves to the same.


The `templates` property is discussed in greater detail [in this article](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/initial-value-templates), and a reference article can be found [here](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/initial-value-templates-api). The rest of this article will deal with the default set of schema types supported in the Sanity Studio.

All schema types are listed below or in the documentation menu.

[**Array** \\
\\
Schema type for arrays of other types.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/array-type) [**Block** \\
\\
Schema type for block which provides a rich text editor for block content.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/block-type) [**Boolean** \\
\\
Schema type reference for expressing truthy values.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/boolean-type) [**Cross-dataset references** \\
\\
All you need to know about creating references across datasets.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/cross-dataset-references) [**Date** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the Date type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/date-type) [**Datetime** \\
\\
The schema type for expressing an exact date and time.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/datetime-type) [**Document** \\
\\
Schema type reference for expressing documents.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/document-type) [**Email** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the email type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/email-type) [**File** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the File type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/file-type) [**Geopoint** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the geopoint type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/geopoint-type) [**Image** \\
\\
Schema type for uploading, selecting, and editing images.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/image-type) [**Number** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the Number type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/number-type) [**Object** \\
\\
Schema type to create custom types to use in a document.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/object-type) [**Reference** \\
\\
A schema type for referencing other documents.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/reference-type) [**Slug** \\
\\
A schema type for slugs is typically used to create unique URLs.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/slug-type) [**String** \\
\\
A schema type for strings and a selectable lists of strings.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/string-type) [**Span** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the Span type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/span-type) [**Text** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the Text type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/text-type) [**URL** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the URL type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/url-type) [**Global document reference** \\
\\
Reference documentation for the \`globalDocumentReference\` schema type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/global-document-reference-type)

[**Properties**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types#k95998f28-7255-47eb-9def-7579c5688282 "Copy link to this section")

- ##### Required [type](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#type-798d15a99732 "Copy link to this section")



string





Name of any valid schema type _._ This will be the type of the value in the data record.

- ##### Required [name](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#name-6761a57a116e "Copy link to this section")



string





The field name. This will be the key in the data record.

- ##### [title](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#title-9bbaa7c16f19 "Copy link to this section")



string





Human readable label for the field.

- ##### [hidden](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#hidden-a6b799ef04e2 "Copy link to this section")



boolean \| () => boolean





Takes a static or a callback function that resolves to a boolean value and hides the given field based on it. You can use this property for conditional fields.

- ##### [readOnly](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#readonly-476941e109de "Copy link to this section")



boolean \| ()=>boolean





If set to `true`, this field will not be editable in the content studio. You can also return a callback function to use it as a conditional field.

- ##### [description](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#description-a91f4a01ca4e "Copy link to this section")

string





Short description to editors how the field is to be used.

- ##### [deprecated](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#deprecated-0a92c2f603c9 "Copy link to this section")



object





Marks a document type or a field as deprecated. This will render the field(s) as read-only with a visual deprecation message defined by the `reason` property.



Example: `deprecated: { reason: 'no longer used' }`



If you deploy a GraphQL API schema, this property will translated into the `@deprecated` directive.

- ##### [options](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#options-646e00663aba "Copy link to this section")



object





A unique set of options depending on the type. See the individual schema type references for available options.

- ##### [validation](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#validation-2fc0ab4b6082 "Copy link to this section")



RuleBuilder





Enables adding one or more validation rules to the field. See the [validation guide](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/validation) for more details, the section below for common validation methods, and the individual schema type references for additional methods.


[**Validation**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types#a80ae6e5-1de7-4692-88f9-845a4a1678fc "Copy link to this section")

- ##### [required()](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#required-eda9af2f2c00 "Copy link to this section")

Ensures the field exists.



Example: `(Rule) => Rule.required()`

- ##### [skip()](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#skip-skip-rule-2543 "Copy link to this section")





Discards the validation rules set before it in the chain and makes the field optional. Rules chained after it still apply.

- ##### [either(\[rule, rule, ...\])](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#either-rule-rule-adcf41d09916 "Copy link to this section")





Accepts an array of rules. If any are truthy, the validation passes.



Example: `(rule) => rule.either([rule.required().min(1), rule.custom((_, context) => context.document?.category !== 'bicycle')])`

- ##### [all(\[rule, rule, ...\])](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#all-rule-rule-c914a2929e5a "Copy link to this section")





Accepts an array of multiple rules, all of which must be true for the validation to pass.



Example: `(rule) => rule.all([rule.required(), rule.custom((value, context) => { ... })])`

- ##### [custom(value, context)](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#custom-value-context-9fd616127457 "Copy link to this section")





Allows for custom validation rules. Receives the field value and the context. Must return true if validation passes, or an error message if validation fails.



Example: `rule => rule.custom(value => { ... })`


**Note**: The properties listed above are common for all data types. For a more thorough description of how to use them, see the individual schema type references.

[**Schema organization tips**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types#k4d55bb107ed4 "Copy link to this section")

The studio loads all schemas defined under `schema.types` in `studio.config.js`.

## OpenAlex Works API

OpenAlex indexes over 320 million scholarly works (journal articles, conference papers, books, datasets, dissertations, preprints, and more), with tens of thousands added daily [1]. Works are the central entity: authors, sources, institutions, topics, and funders all connect through them [1].

**API base:** `api.openalex.org/works`  
**Single-work lookup:** `api.openalex.org/works/W2741809807`  
**OpenAlex work ID format:** `W` followed by a numeric string (e.g., `W2741809807`) [1]

Linked entity types on a work record: authorships, locations, topics, keywords, funders, awards [1].

### Data sources

OpenAlex was seeded by the Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG, discontinued 2021) and Crossref, with additional ingestion from DataCite, PubMed, HAL, and institutional/subject repositories [1].

### Deduplication: how locations become works

OpenAlex starts from *locations* — individual hosted copies of a work (e.g., an arXiv preprint, a published journal version, a repository accepted manuscript). Two mechanisms identify that multiple locations are the same work [1]:

1. **Persistent identifiers (PIDs).** A shared DOI, PubMed ID, or arXiv ID is treated as proof of identity; the location joins the existing work and enriches it.
2. **Fuzzy metadata matching.** Locations with no shared PID go through title normalization plus author-name matching. If nothing matches, a new work record is seeded. Locations with neither a PID nor a usable title are dropped.

API supports filter, search, sort, group, and paginate over all work attributes [1].

---

## Crossref REST API

**Base URL:** `https://api.crossref.org/`  
**Authentication:** No sign-up required; almost all metadata is free of copyright and can be used for any purpose. Some abstracts may be subject to publisher/author copyright [2]. Use the polite pool by adding `mailto=yourmail@company.org` as a query parameter [2].

Available metadata beyond bibliographic basics: funding data, license information, post-publication updates, ORCID identifiers, ROR IDs, abstracts [2].

### Endpoints

| Endpoint | Returns |
|---|---|
| `/works` | List of registered content items (many filters available) |
| `/works/{doi}` | Single metadata record for a Crossref DOI |
| `/works/{doi}/agency` | Registration agency for the DOI (e.g., Crossref or DataCite) |
| `/journals` | Journals with registered content |
| `/journals/{issn}` | Details for a specific journal |
| `/journals/{issn}/works` | Works in a given journal |
| `/members` | All organisations that have registered metadata |
| `/members/{id}/works/` | Works associated with a member |
| `/prefixes/{prefix}` | Steward name and member ID for a DOI prefix |
| `/prefixes/{prefix}/works` | Works associated with a prefix |
| `/funders` | Funders in the Open Funder Registry |
| `/funders/{id}/works` | Works associated with a funder ID |
| `/types` | All work types (e.g., `journal-article`, `monograph`, `grant`) |
| `/licenses` | Licenses used by registered content items |

Results returned in JSON; content negotiation available for single-record formats [2].

DOI lookup example: `https://api.crossref.org/works/doi/10.1128/mbio.01735-25` [2]

Metadata is deposited by member publishers and complemented by trusted sources such as Retraction Watch [2].

---

## Metadata standards: author, affiliation, funding, and integrity (Crossref + DataCite)

The Crossref/DataCite integrity metadata framework covers actors and relationships beyond the DOI alone [3]. Key metadata dimensions:

- **Author attribution:** contributor names and roles
- **Affiliations:** institutional identifiers (ROR IDs) linked to authors
- **Funding:** funder names and grant identifiers; as of September 2026, funder names deposited without an identifier are matched to ROR IDs automatically [2]
- **Dates:** submission, acceptance, publication, and update timestamps
- **Related objects:** links between outputs (datasets, preprints, publications)
- **Rights:** license information

**Limitation:** metadata is declared by depositors and may be incomplete or incorrect; presence of metadata is not a guarantee of scientific quality, and absence of a notice is not proof of absence of correction [3].

---

## Versioning, corrections, and retractions (Crossref)

Crossref distinguishes three version types [4]:

- **Preprint:** a version before peer review and formal publication
- **Version of record (VoR):** the formally published, peer-reviewed version
- **Update notification:** a correction, retraction, expression-of-concern, or other post-publication change linked to the original record

The versioning framework links versions to each other so that a corrected or retracted record retains its trace — the original record is not erased, only annotated. Metadata for updates depends on what member publishers deposit; absence of an update notice in Crossref metadata does not prove no correction exists [4].

When evaluating a source retrieved via DOI, check `/works/{doi}` for `update-to` and `is-referenced-by-count` fields, and consult the Crossref Crossmark service for post-publication status signals.

Documentation Menu

## REST API

[Metadata Retrieval](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/) [Access and authentication](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/rest-api/access-and-authentication/)

Our publicly available REST API exposes the scholarly metadata that members and trusted sources deposit with Crossref. This bibliographic metadata and much more—you will find funding data, license information, post-publication updates, ORCID and ROR IDs, and abstracts. You can search, facet, filter, or sample metadata from dozens of thousands of members from all around the world, and the results are returned in JSON format.

The metadata is deposited directly by our members, who publish the content represented by each metadata record. This is complemented by trusted sources, such as [Retraction Watch](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/retraction-watch/). You will also find other identifiers, such as ORCID for individuals, RORs for funders and affiliations, and more. In some cases we add these identifiers where they are missing in the original deposit. There is an overview of the available content at [Crossref stats](https://www.crossref.org/06members/53status.html).

No sign-up is required to use the REST API, and almost none of the metadata is subject to copyright, and you may use it for any purpose. Some abstracts contained in the metadata may be subject to copyright by publishers or authors.

## Quick start

Use [https://api.crossref.org/](https://api.crossref.org/) as your base URL. Add one of the available endpoints to query works, journals, members, funders, licences, prefixes, or types. Here are some examples to get you started:

| I would like to… | Example request |
| --- | --- |
| Use the polite pool | [https://api.crossref.org/works?rows=0&mailto=yourmail@company.org](https://api.crossref.org/works?rows=0&mailto=yourmail@company.org) |
| Retrieve metadata for a Crossref DOI | [https://api.crossref.org/works/doi/10.1128/mbio.01735-25](https://api.crossref.org/works/doi/10.1128/mbio.01735-25) |
| Retrieve records for 10 content items | [https://api.crossref.org/works?rows=10](https://api.crossref.org/works?rows=10) |
| Find works in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology, ISSN 03064530 | [https://api.crossref.org/journals/03064530/works](https://api.crossref.org/journals/03064530/works) |

## Endpoints

The Crossref REST API provides a number of endpoints for querying different types of records. Each endpoint has request parameters and [filters](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/rest-api/rest-api-filters/) to enable you to retrieve the metadata you are looking for. For further details about each endpoint, its parameters, and to try them out, see the Swagger documentation at [https://api.crossref.org/](https://api.crossref.org/)

| Endpoint | Metadata returned |
| --- | --- |
| **/works** | A list of content items registered with Crossref. This endpoint has a large number of parameters and [filters](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/rest-api/rest-api-filters/) available. |
| /works/{doi} | A single metadata record for a Crossref DOI. |
| /works/{doi}/agency | The registration agency for the specified DOI (e.g., Crossref or DataCite). |
| **/journals** | A list of journals whose content with registered content items. |
| /journals/{issn} | Details of the journal with the given ISSN. |
| /journals/{issn}/works | A list of works in the journal with the given ISSN. |
| **members** | A list of all organisations that have registered metadata with Crossref. |
| /members/{id} | Details about the Crossref member with the specified member ID. |
| /members/{id}/works/ | A list of works associated with the specified member. |
| **/prefixes**/{prefix} | The name and Crossref member ID of the steward of the specified prefix. |
| /prefixes/{prefix}/works | A list of works associated with the specified prefix. |
| **/funders** | A list of funders in the Open Funder Registry. |
| /funders/{id} | Metadata for the member with the given ID. |
| /funders/{id}/works | A list of works associated with the specified funder ID. |
| **/types** | A list of all work types used in Crossref metadata. |
| /types/{id} | Information about the specified work type, e.g. `journal-article`, `monograph`, `grant`. |
| /types/{id}/works | A list of works with the specified work type. |
| **/licenses** | A list of licenses used by registered content items. |

## Content negotiation

The REST API can return single metadata records in a variety of formats through a process known as content negotiation. See the [content negotiation](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/content-negotiation/) page for more details.

## Report an issue

Have you detected something that you would like to report? It could be incorrect, confusing, or partial metadata. Please report it on our [community forum](https://community.crossref.org/) or check our [backlog](https://crossref.atlassian.net/jira/software/c/projects/CR/issues) of bugs and feature requests to see if it has already been reported.

Eg: [W2741809807](https://openalex.org/works/W2741809807)Count: [327,124,722](https://openalex.org/works)Links:[authorships](https://help.openalex.org/data/authorships/), [locations](https://help.openalex.org/data/locations/), [topics](https://help.openalex.org/data/topics/), [keywords](https://help.openalex.org/data/keywords/), [funders](https://help.openalex.org/data/funders/), [awards](https://help.openalex.org/data/awards/)

A **work** is any scholarly document: a journal article, conference paper, book or book chapter, dataset, dissertation, preprint, and more. There are over 320 million works in OpenAlex, with tens of thousands added every day. A work’s OpenAlex ID looks like `W2741809807`; fetch one at [`api.openalex.org/works/W2741809807`](https://api.openalex.org/works/W2741809807).

Works are the central entity in OpenAlex — everything connects to them. [Authors](https://help.openalex.org/data/authors/) write works, [sources](https://help.openalex.org/data/sources/) publish them, [institutions](https://help.openalex.org/data/institutions/) get credit for them, [topics](https://help.openalex.org/data/topics/) describe them, and [funders](https://help.openalex.org/data/funders/) pay for them. Works also carry by far the most information of any entity: all twenty-ish entity types are first-class citizens, but works are the firstest class.

## About [Link to this section](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/\#about)

### Where works come from [Link to this section](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/\#where-works-come-from)

OpenAlex aggregates and builds on many open data sources. The catalog was seeded by the [Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Academic) — Microsoft Research’s effort to catalog the scholarly literature — whose final open dataset OpenAlex adopted when the project was discontinued in 2021. The other primary source is [Crossref](https://www.crossref.org/), the open DOI-registration agency. Alongside those, works are drawn from DataCite, PubMed, HAL, institutional and subject repositories, and more; see [How it’s built](https://help.openalex.org/data/how-its-built/) for the full ingest picture.

### How locations become works [Link to this section](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/\#how-locations-become-works)

OpenAlex starts from [locations](https://help.openalex.org/data/locations/): copies of a work hosted at particular places. A preprint on arXiv is one location; the same paper published in _Physical Review B_ is a second; the accepted manuscript in a university repository is a third. The job is to recognize that all three are one work. Two mechanisms do that, used together:

- **Persistent identifiers.** If a location carries a DOI, PubMed ID, or arXiv ID that OpenAlex already knows, it belongs to that work. This is the certain path: a shared PID is treated as proof.
- **Fuzzy metadata matching.** Locations with no shared PID — most repository copies, many preprints — go through a fuzzy matching algorithm built on title normalization plus author names, tuned over the years for precision and recall.

Whichever path matches, the location joins the existing work and _enriches_ it rather than minting a new one. If nothing matches, the location seeds a new work of its own; the only locations that don’t are ones with neither a PID nor a usable title, which are dropped.

Once a work exists, OpenAlex tracks its own metadata — title, abstract (and often full text), publication date, type — and the connections that make it useful at scale: authors, institutional affiliations, the source it appeared in, topics, funders, and citations.

How works cite each other — references, citation counts, and FWCI — has its own page: [Citations](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/citations/). How OpenAlex decides whether a work is free to read: [Open access](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/open-access/).

## In the API [Link to this section](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/\#in-the-api)

The Works endpoint is at [`api.openalex.org/works`](https://api.openalex.org/works). Fetch a single work by ID — [`/works/W2741809807`](https://api.openalex.org/works/W2741809807) — or a list, and [filter](https://help.openalex.org/api/filtering/), [search](https://help.openalex.org/api/searching/), [sort](https://help.openalex.org/api/sorting/), [group](https://help.openalex.org/api/grouping/), and [page](https://help.openalex.org/api/paging/) over the attributes documented on the [Attributes](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/attributes/) page. For the full list of endpoints see the [endpoints index](https://help.openalex.org/api/endpoints/).

entries.body:
Exa exposes two primary endpoints — `POST /search` and `POST /contents` — plus an Agent API for long-running research tasks. Authentication uses an `x-api-key` header (or `Authorization: Bearer`). SDKs are available for Python (`exa_py`) and JavaScript (`exa-js`).

## Search endpoint (`POST /search`)

`query` (string, required) is the only mandatory field. Write queries in natural language; include the subject, source type, and time period when relevant. Avoid terse terms like `"news"` — `"Latest news on EU battery policy"` gives Exa enough intent to rank well [1].

Search returns up to 10 results by default (`numResults`, max 100; contact sales for higher limits) [2]. No pagination is supported [1].

### Search types

`type` selects the retrieval mode. `auto` is the default [1][2]:

| Type | Use it when | Typical latency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `auto` | Best default balance of quality and speed | ~1 second |
| `fast` | Latency-sensitive, user-facing search | ~450 ms |
| `instant` | Real-time path (autocomplete, voice) | ~250 ms |
| `deep-lite` | Lightweight research + synthesis | ~4 seconds |
| `deep` | Multi-step search + stronger synthesis | 4–15 seconds |
| `deep-reasoning` | Completeness and reasoning depth over latency | 12–40 seconds |

Deep modes run a multi-step research process rather than a single retrieval pass. `additionalQueries` (1–10 strings) can be passed alongside the main query for broader deep-search results [2]. For long-running research, list building, and multi-hop enrichment, prefer Exa Agent over `deep-reasoning` [1].

### Filters

Filters are hard constraints; softer source preferences belong in the query text [1].

- **`includeDomains`** / **`excludeDomains`**: accept full hostnames (`arxiv.org`), path prefixes (`anthropic.com/news`), or wildcard subdomains (`*.substack.com`). Up to 1,200 entries each. Use these instead of `site:` in the query [2].
- **`startPublishedDate`** / **`endPublishedDate`**: ISO 8601 date-time strings to filter by publication date [2].
- **`category`**: focus results on `company`, `publication`, `news`, `personal site`, `financial report`, or `people`. The `publication` category surfaces scholarly papers with structured metadata (authors, venue, citations). Note: `company` and `people` categories do **not** support `startPublishedDate`, `endPublishedDate`, or `excludeDomains` — using them returns a 400 error [2].
- **`userLocation`**: two-letter ISO country code (e.g. `"US"`) [2].
- **`moderation`**: boolean, default `false`; filters unsafe content from results [2].
- **`compliance`**: enterprise-only; set to `"hipaa"` for HIPAA mode (cache-only retrieval) [2].

### Output shapes (contents)

All three modes are nested inside the `contents` object on `/search` (on `/contents` they are top-level):

- **`highlights: true`** — query-relevant excerpts sized per result. Recommended for agents and RAG; keeps context smaller than full text [1]. Dynamic Highlights achieves a 40% average token efficiency gain relative to earlier highlights, with quality increase [3].
- **`text: { maxCharacters: N }`** — full clean page body as markdown. Use when document structure or broad context matters. Apply `maxCharacters` to control size [1].
- **`summary: { query, schema? }`** — LLM call per page producing prose or JSON-schema-structured output. Adds cost per result [1][3].

Pick **one** view per request — requesting multiple returns and bills each separately [1].

### Output schema (synthesis)

`outputSchema` synthesizes search results into a structured response. Supported root types are `"text"` (freeform prose with `description`) and `"object"` (JSON following your schema). Object schemas support up to 2 levels of nesting and 10 properties. The synthesized value appears in `output.content`; field-level sources and confidence scores are in `output.grounding`. Works with every search type; adds ~2 seconds of synthesis latency on top of the selected type. Streaming via `stream: true` is available only when `outputSchema` is provided [1][2].

Use `systemPrompt` for behavioral instructions (source preferences, duplication avoidance); use `outputSchema` for shape [1].

### Content freshness

`contents.maxAgeHours` controls how fresh extracted page content must be (does not filter results by publication date) [1]:

| Value | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Omit | Use cached content when available, fetch when needed |
| Positive integer | Use cache if newer than N hours, else fetch live |
| `0` | Always fetch fresh content |
| `-1` | Only use cached content |

Pair with `livecrawlTimeout` (milliseconds, default 10000) to cap live fetch time; raise to 12000–15000 for slow sites [3]. The deprecated `livecrawl` string parameter (`"always"`, `"never"`, etc.) is superseded by `maxAgeHours` [3].

## Contents endpoint (`POST /contents`)

Accepts `ids` or `urls` (interchangeable: page URLs or `id` values from a search response). Handles JavaScript-rendered pages, PDFs, and complex layouts automatically [3].

Content options sit at the top level (no `contents` wrapper) alongside `ids`. The same three modes apply: `highlights`, `text`, and `summary`. Passing a `highlights.query` focuses extraction on a specific aspect of the page [3].

Content extraction is **free for up to 10 results per `/search` call**; beyond that it is **$1 per 1,000 pages**. Exa recommends using `/search` with `contents` enabled rather than `/contents` for web search tool use cases [3].

Additional `/contents` parameters:
- **`subpages: N`** — follow links from each URL, crawling up to N subpages. Use `subpageTarget` (array of strings) to prioritize site sections [3].
- **`extras.imageLinks: N`** — return up to N image URLs per page; results also include `favicon` and a representative `image` URL [3].
- **`maxAgeHours`** and **`livecrawlTimeout`** work identically to `/search` [3].

### Common `/contents` mistakes

| Instead of | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `contents: { text: ... }` wrapper | Top-level `text`, `highlights`, `summary` |
| `useAutoprompt` | Remove — no query to rewrite |
| `stream: true` | Not supported on `/contents` |
| `numSentences`, `highlightsPerUrl` | `highlights: true`; use `highlights.maxCharacters` for fixed limits |
| `tokensNum` | `text.maxCharacters` |
| `livecrawl: "always"` | `maxAgeHours: 0` (don't send both) |
| `crawledBeforeDate` | `snapshotAsOf` |
| `context: true` | `highlights` or `text`; build context from `results[]` |

## Response cost structure

The `costDollars` object in every response breaks down costs by component: `search.neural`, `search.keyword`, `summary`, `contents.text`, `contents.highlights`, `contents.summary`. Billing is computed from usage counters, not the response object itself [2].

Exa Contents returns clean page content from URLs, handling JavaScript-rendered pages, PDFs, and complex layouts automatically.All contents features are also available in [Exa Search](https://exa.ai/docs/search/quickstart) for returned URLs, at no extra charge up to 10 results per search ($1/1000 pages afterwards). We recommend using Search in this way instead of Contents for web search tool use cases.

For search results feeding AI context, request `contents: { highlights: true }` on `/search` —
Exa sizes each result’s excerpts to its relevance. See [Highlights](https://exa.ai/docs/search/highlights).

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/contents/quickstart\#make-your-first-request)  Make your first request

Pass one or more URLs or document IDs and request highlights for the parts relevant to your task. In HTTP requests, provide them in `ids`:

Python

}'
```

To extract fields instead of prose, pass a JSON schema in `summary.schema`. The summary comes
back as a JSON string matching the schema; parse it to read the fields:

```
{
  "ids": ["https://example.com/company"],
  "summary": {
    "schema": {
      "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
      "title": "Company Information",
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "name": { "type": "string", "description": "The company name" },
        "industry": { "type": "string", "description": "Primary industry" },
        "foundedYear": { "type": "number", "description": "Year the company was founded" }
      },
      "required": ["name"]
    }
  }
}
```

Pick one content view per request. Requesting highlights, text, and summary together returns and bills each view separately.

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/contents/quickstart\#content-freshness)  Content freshness

`maxAgeHours` controls how fresh the extracted page content must be.

| Value | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Omit | Use cached content when available and fetch the page when needed |
| Positive integer | Use cached content if it is newer than this many hours, otherwise fetch the page |
| `0` | Always fetch fresh content |
| `-1` | Only use cached content |

Most requests should omit this field. Set it when stale page content would be unusable, such as for prices, availability, or frequently updated pages. Pair a low `maxAgeHours` with `livecrawlTimeout` (milliseconds) to cap how long a fresh fetch may take.

Migrate from the deprecated livecrawl parameter

The `livecrawl` string parameter (`"always"`, `"preferred"`, `"fallback"`, `"never"`) is
deprecated in favor of `maxAgeHours`:

| Old `livecrawl` value | Equivalent |
| --- | --- |
| `"always"` | `maxAgeHours: 0` |
| `"never"` | `maxAgeHours: -1` |
| `"fallback"` | Omit `maxAgeHours` |
| `"preferred"` | No direct equivalent; use a low value such as `maxAgeHours: 1` |

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/contents/quickstart\#crawl-subpages)  Crawl subpages

Set `subpages` to follow links from each starting URL. Add `subpageTarget` when you want Exa to prioritize particular site sections:

Python

JavaScript

cURL

```
result = exa.get_contents(
    ["https://docs.example.com"],
    subpages=10,
    subpage_target=["api", "reference", "guides"],
    highlights=True,
)
```

```
const result = await exa.getContents(
  ["https://docs.example.com"],
  {
    subpages: 10,
    subpageTarget: ["api", "reference", "guides"],
    highlights: true
  }
);
```

```
curl -s -X POST "https://api.exa.ai/contents" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $EXA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "ids": ["https://docs.example.com"],
    "subpages": 10,
    "subpageTarget": ["api", "reference", "guides"],
    "highlights": true
  }'
```

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/contents/quickstart\#images-and-favicons)  Images and favicons

Set `extras.imageLinks` to the number of image URLs you want from each page. Results also include
the site’s `favicon` and a representative `image` URL when available. On `/search`, this option
sits at `contents.extras.imageLinks`.

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/contents/quickstart\#common-mistakes)  Common mistakes

`/contents` shares most of its options with `/search` but places them differently, and requests copied from older examples often carry parameters this endpoint never had. The [API reference](https://exa.ai/docs/reference/get-contents) is the source of truth for the current schema.

| Instead of | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `contents: { text: ... }` | Top-level `text`, `highlights`, and `summary`. Unlike `/search`, `/contents` has no `contents` wrapper. |
| `useAutoprompt` | Nothing. There is no query to rewrite on `/contents`; remove the field. |
| `stream: true` | A normal request. `/contents` does not support streaming. |
| `numSentences`, `highlightsPerUrl` | `highlights: true`. Exa sizes highlights to each page; set `highlights.maxCharacters` only for a fixed excerpt limit. |
| `tokensNum` | `text.maxCharacters`. |
| `livecrawl: "always"` | `maxAgeHours: 0`. Do not send `livecrawl` and `maxAgeHours` together. |
| `crawledBeforeDate` | `snapshotAsOf`. |
| `context: true` | `highlights` or `text`; build the context string from `results[]`. |

A few behaviors that are easy to miss:

- `urls` and `ids` are interchangeable. Pass either the page URLs or the `id` values from a search response.
- A fresh fetch (`maxAgeHours: 0` or a low value) waits up to `livecrawlTimeout` milliseconds (default 10000). Raise it to 12000–15000 for slow sites, or lower it when latency matters more than freshness.
- The Python SDK uses snake\_case for every key: `exa.get_contents(urls, highlights=True, max_age_hours=24)`.

RUN_ID="$(curl -s -X POST "https://api.exa.ai/agent/runs" \

  -d '{

    "effort": "medium"
  }' | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["id"])')"

while true; do
  RUN_JSON="$(curl -s "https://api.exa.ai/agent/runs/$RUN_ID" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $EXA_API_KEY")"
  STATUS="$(printf '%s' "$RUN_JSON" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["status"])')"

  if [ "$STATUS" = "completed" ]; then
    printf '%s' "$RUN_JSON" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["output"]["text"])'

  elif [ "$STATUS" = "failed" ] || [ "$STATUS" = "cancelled" ]; then
    printf '%s' "$RUN_JSON"
    break
  fi

  sleep 4
done

See [What’s in Exa’s Index](https://exa.ai/docs/search/data/overview) for what Exa’s index includes and how to search those content types.

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/search/quickstart\#search-types)  Choose a search type

`type` selects a search mode, each tuned for a different balance of speed, search depth, and synthesis. `auto` is the default and works for most searches.

| Type | Use it when | Typical latency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `auto` | You want the best default balance of quality and speed | ~1 second |
| `fast` | The request is latency-sensitive | ~450 ms |
| `instant` | The request is on a real-time path such as autocomplete or voice | ~250 ms |
| `deep-lite` | The task needs lightweight research and synthesis | ~4 seconds |
| `deep` | The task requires multi-step search and stronger synthesis | 4–15 seconds |
| `deep-reasoning` | Completeness and reasoning depth matter more than latency | 12–40 seconds |

Latency figures are approximate and cover the search itself with cached content. `outputSchema` adds a synthesis step and a low `contents.maxAgeHours` adds a fresh page fetch; see [Budget latency and context](https://exa.ai/docs/search/best-practices#budget-latency-and-context).Deep modes run a research process rather than a single retrieval pass. See [Deep Search](https://exa.ai/docs/search/deep-search) for how that process works and how to use its additional controls.

building, and multi-hop enrichment. Agent has more compute per run and returns grounded,
structured results.

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/search/quickstart\#output-shapes)  Output shapes

Every result includes metadata such as its title, URL, and publication date. Use `contents` to add highlights, full text, or a summary from the page.

- Highlights

- Full text


Highlights return the excerpts most relevant to your query. They give models and agents the
evidence they need without filling the context window with unrelated parts of each page.This is the recommended output shape for most tasks.Start with bare `highlights: true`. Exa uses the query to select an appropriate amount of
content from each result.

Python

JavaScript

cURL

```
result = exa.search(
    "How are inference providers reducing transformer latency?",
    contents={"highlights": True},
)
```

```
const result = await exa.search(
  "How are inference providers reducing transformer latency?",
  { contents: { highlights: true } }
);
```

```
curl -s -X POST "https://api.exa.ai/search" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $EXA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "query": "How are inference providers reducing transformer latency?",
    "contents": { "highlights": true }
  }'
```

See [Highlights](https://exa.ai/docs/search/highlights) for Dynamic Highlights and guidance on when to enable it.

Full text returns the clean page body. Use it when the task depends on broader context, document
structure, or details that may fall outside query-focused excerpts.Full pages can be large. Limit both the number of results and the text returned per page.

Python

JavaScript

cURL

same fields sit at the top level next to `urls`: `"urls": [...], "highlights": true`

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/search/quickstart\#output-schema)  Output schema

Add `outputSchema` when you want Exa to synthesize the search results. It works with every search type and adds an `output` object to the response.The ranked pages remain in `results`. The generated value is returned in `output.content`, with field-level sources and confidence in `output.grounding`.

- Freeform Text

- Structured JSON


Use `type: "text"` for generated prose. Add a `description` to specify its format or length.

Python

JavaScript

cURL

```
result = exa.search(
    "What changed in the latest EU battery policy?",
    output_schema={
        "type": "text",
        "description": "Summarize the changes in three concise bullets",
    },
)
```

```
const result = await exa.search(
  "What changed in the latest EU battery policy?",
  {
    outputSchema: {
      type: "text",
      description: "Summarize the changes in three concise bullets"
    }

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/search/quickstart\#filter-results)  Filter results

Filters are hard constraints: add one when a result outside it would be unusable to you, and keep softer source preferences in the query text instead. The [API reference](https://exa.ai/docs/reference/search) has the full set.

### [​](https://exa.ai/docs/search/quickstart\#include-domains-or-paths)  Include domains or paths

`includeDomains` restricts results to sources you trust. It accepts full domains, path prefixes such as `anthropic.com/news`, and subdomain wildcards such as `*.substack.com`.

Python

JavaScript

cURL

```
result = exa.search(
    "new model releases",
    include_domains=["openai.com", "anthropic.com/news"],
    contents={"highlights": True},
)
```

```
const result = await exa.search("new model releases", {
  includeDomains: ["openai.com", "anthropic.com/news"],
  contents: { highlights: true }
});
```

```
curl -s -X POST "https://api.exa.ai/search" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $EXA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "query": "new model releases",
    "includeDomains": ["openai.com", "anthropic.com/news"],
    "contents": { "highlights": true }
  }'
```

Put the path in the filter rather than repeating it as a `site:` operator in the query.

### [​](https://exa.ai/docs/search/quickstart\#exclude-domains-or-paths)  Exclude domains or paths

`excludeDomains` removes results from specific domains or paths. It supports the same path prefixes and subdomain wildcards as `includeDomains`. Use it when those sources would make a result unusable, not to express a preference.

JavaScript

cURL

```
result = exa.search(
    "primary research on retrieval-augmented generation benchmarks",
    exclude_domains=["medium.com", "dev.to"],
    contents={"highlights": True},
)
```

const result = await exa.search(
  "primary research on retrieval-augmented generation benchmarks",
  {
    excludeDomains: ["medium.com", "dev.to"],

    "query": "primary research on retrieval-augmented generation benchmarks",
    "excludeDomains": ["medium.com", "dev.to"],
    "contents": { "highlights": true }

```

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/search/quickstart\#content-freshness)  Content freshness

`contents.maxAgeHours` controls how fresh the content extracted from each result must be. It does not filter results by publication date.

| Value | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Omit | Use cached content when available and fetch the page when needed |
| Positive integer | Use cached content if it is newer than this many hours; otherwise fetch the page |
| `0` | Always fetch fresh content |
| `-1` | Only use cached content |

Most searches should omit this field. Set it when stale page content would be unusable, such as for prices, availability, or a page that changes frequently.

Python

JavaScript

cURL

```
result = exa.search(
    "current pricing for serverless GPU providers",
    contents={
        "highlights": True,
        "max_age_hours": 24,
    },
)

```

  contents: {
    highlights: true,
    maxAgeHours: 24

});

    "query": "current pricing for serverless GPU providers",
    "contents": {
      "highlights": true,
      "maxAgeHours": 24
    }
  }'
```

entries.body:
Seven document parsing and conversion tools complement Firecrawl's web scraping when dealing with PDFs and structured scholarly documents. Firecrawl's own scrape/crawl/map endpoints are covered at `search_and_retrieval/firecrawl/endpoints`.

## Docling (IBM Research AI4K)

Docling converts PDFs into typed JSON or Markdown via a modular pipeline: it joins programmatic PDF tokens and coordinates, applies layout prediction, recovers table structure, optionally runs OCR, and assembles a final document object [1]. The pipeline handles reading order explicitly. Code is MIT-licensed. Docling is best suited for digitally born PDFs with complex layouts; OCR is optional and some speed/quality tradeoffs are backend-dependent. Reported performance benchmarks used a 225-page sample with OCR disabled and are not Orbit measurements [1].

## Nougat (Meta AI)

Nougat (Neural Optical Understanding for Academic Documents) converts rendered scientific-document page images into markup, including mathematical expressions [3]. It operates visually — page images in, markup out — making it suitable for papers where equations and symbols are rendered rather than encoded as text. Known limitations (Section 5.5 of the ICLR 2024 paper): repetition loops during generation, poor handling of non-Latin scripts, and inconsistencies across independently processed pages (processing is page-independent, so context from adjacent pages is not used) [3]. Training corpus is predominantly English research papers; inference speed depends on hardware and page text density [3].

## SmolDocling (IBM Research, 2025)

SmolDocling is a 256M-parameter vision-language model for end-to-end multimodal document conversion [7]. It introduces **DocTags**, a structured output format that separates text from structural tags, encodes nested captions/lists and table structure, and includes spatial location information for each element [7]. Its compact size is the primary design goal. Author-reported performance figures are available; independent deployment and resource requirements are unverified. Schema richness does not guarantee accurate predictions [7].

## pypdf

pypdf extracts digitally encoded text directly from PDF content streams [2]. It is **not** OCR software and cannot extract text from image-only or scanned PDFs; it also cannot detect or correct OCR mistakes already embedded in a file. Key caveats: complex coordinate handling, table structure, and reading-order interpretation may be wrong or ambiguous; content-stream memory limits apply to very large files [2]. pypdf is the right choice when the PDF has a genuine text layer (digitally born); for scanned or mixed-content files, pair it with OCRmyPDF or use a model-based tool.

## OCRmyPDF

OCRmyPDF adds a searchable OCR text layer to scanned or mixed-content PDFs while preserving source appearance where possible [4]. It uses Tesseract as the underlying OCR engine. Limitations: OCR output can be gibberish on poor-quality scans; Tesseract does not supply paragraph or heading structure and may join columns incorrectly; reading order is not guaranteed [4]. Dependency note: the documentation contains an internal inconsistency — the v17 section states Ghostscript is no longer strictly required, while the final paragraph says it is required. Verify against a pinned version before adopting [4].

## GROBID

GROBID (GeneRation Of BIbliographic Data) extracts structured scholarly-document metadata — sections, references, and annotations — and outputs TEI XML using a customized TEI schema [5]. It distinguishes between XML well-formedness and schema validation; validation failures are treated as possible evidence of problematic extraction [5]. Important boundary: well-formedness and schema validity do not establish semantic accuracy of the extracted content. The official documentation uses historical examples; the exact deployed GROBID version and behavior should be verified against a pinned release [5].

## PubTables-1M (Microsoft, CVPR 2022)

PubTables-1M is a dataset and modeling framework for table detection, structure recognition, and functional analysis in unstructured documents [6]. It addresses **oversegmentation** as a ground-truth annotation ambiguity and canonicalizes header/cell representations; annotations retain spatial locations and structural roles [6]. Detection alone cannot validate cell values or header meaning. The benchmark corpus is scientific tables from PubMed Central; performance on that corpus does not establish correctness on arbitrary Orbit documents [6].

## Selection guidance

| Tool | Input | Output | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Docling | PDF (born-digital or scanned) | JSON / Markdown | Layout-aware document conversion |
| Nougat | Page images | Markup (with math) | Scientific papers with equations |
| SmolDocling | Page images | DocTags | Lightweight multimodal conversion |
| pypdf | Born-digital PDF | Plain text | Fast text extraction, no OCR needed |
| OCRmyPDF | Scanned/mixed PDF | PDF + text layer | Adding searchability to scanned files |
| GROBID | Scholarly PDF | TEI XML | Reference and metadata extraction |
| PubTables-1M | Document images | Table structure | Table detection and structure recovery |

entries.body:
Firecrawl exposes three primary endpoints — `/scrape`, `/crawl`, and `/map` — all at `https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/`. SDK packages: `firecrawl-py` (Python), `firecrawl` (Node). An API key adds higher rate limits; basic usage works without one.

---

## /scrape — Single URL to clean content

`POST /v2/scrape` converts one URL into clean content. Auto-detects PDFs and DOCX from the URL, handling them transparently. For local files not accessible by URL, use `/parse` instead [1].

### Output formats

Pass an array of format strings (or objects for JSON) in the `formats` field [1]:

| Format | Description |
|---|---|
| `markdown` | Cleaned markdown (default LLM target) |
| `summary` | Summarised text |
| `html` | Cleaned HTML |
| `rawHtml` | Unmodified HTML as received |
| `rawBase64` | Base64-encoded HTTP response body; must be the **only** format in the request |
| `screenshot` / `screenshot@fullPage` | Screenshot URL (expires 24 h); `quality` and `viewport` options available |
| `links` | All links extracted from the page |
| `json` | Structured extraction via JSON Schema or free-text `prompt` |
| `images` | All image URLs from the page |
| `branding` | Brand identity: colors, fonts, typography, spacing, UI components |
| `product` | Structured product fields (title, price, availability, variants) — no LLM call, no schema needed |
| `audio` | MP3 audio from supported video URLs (e.g. YouTube); returns signed GCS URL, expires 1 h |
| `video` | Best-quality video from supported video URLs; signed GCS URL, expires 1 h |
| `query` | Natural-language question; answer returned in `answer` field (`prompt` and optional `mode`) |

`rawBase64` is incompatible with any other format; the API rejects combined requests. `product` is preferred over `json` for product pages — deterministic, no schema definition required [1].

### Response status layers

Two separate layers [1]:
- **API status**: HTTP `200` + `success: true` means Firecrawl accepted and processed the request, even if the target page errored.
- **Page status**: `data.metadata.statusCode` — the HTTP status from the target site. Firecrawl treats `2xx` or `304` as a clean load; anything else means the page did not load cleanly.

### Credit costs (scrape) [1]

| Option | Additional credits |
|---|---|
| Base scrape | 1 credit/page |
| JSON mode | +4 credits/page |
| Question / highlights formats | +4 credits/page/format |
| PII redaction | +4 credits/page |
| PDF parsing | +1 credit/PDF page |
| Audio or video extraction | +4 credits/page |
| Zero Data Retention (ZDR) | +1 credit/page |

### Caching and maxAge [2]

- Default freshness window: `maxAge = 172800000` ms (2 days). Cached pages newer than this are returned instantly; otherwise a fresh scrape is done.
- Speed improvement: up to 5× faster for cached results.
- `maxAge: 0` — bypass cache entirely (slower, higher failure risk).
- `storeInCache: false` — prevent Firecrawl from caching this request's results.
- `minAge` — cache-only lookup; if no cached data exists, returns `404` with `SCRAPE_NO_CACHED_DATA`. Set to `1` to accept any cached data.
- Requests using `changeTracking` bypass the cache (`maxAge` is ignored).
- Cached results still cost **1 credit per page** — caching improves speed, not credit usage.

### Batch scraping [2]

`POST /v2/batch/scrape` submits multiple URLs in one job. Works like `/crawl`: returns a job ID for async polling (`GET /v2/batch/scrape/{id}`), or use the SDK's synchronous method to wait for all results. Batch scrape jobs expire after **24 hours** [2].

### Zero Data Retention (ZDR) [2]

Set `zeroDataRetention: true` in the request. Firecrawl will not persist page content or extracted data beyond the request lifetime. Requires an **Enterprise plan**. Screenshots are incompatible with ZDR (requires persistent storage) — requests combining both return an error. Costs +1 credit/page.

### Location and language targeting [2]

Include a `location` object with:
- `country`: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code (e.g. `'US'`, `'DE'`, `'JP'`). Defaults to `'US'`.
- `languages`: array of preferred languages in priority order. Defaults to the language of the specified country.

Firecrawl selects an appropriate proxy and emulates the corresponding locale and timezone [2].

---

## /crawl — Recursive site crawling

`POST /v2/crawl` submits a URL and recursively discovers and scrapes every reachable subpage. All scrape options (formats, proxy, caching, actions, location) apply to every page via `scrapeOptions` (JS) / `scrape_options` (Python). Returns a job ID for polling [3].

Default `limit` is 10,000 pages. Before starting, the endpoint checks that remaining credits can cover `limit`; if not, returns **402 Payment Required**. Set a lower `limit` to match your intended crawl size [3].

### Configuration reference [4]

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `url` | string | required | Starting URL |
| `limit` | integer | `10000` | Max pages to crawl |
| `maxDiscoveryDepth` | integer | — | Link-discovery hops from root. Root + sitemapped pages = depth 0. Pages at max depth are scraped but their links are not followed. |
| `includePaths` | string[] | — | Pathname regex patterns to include (Rust/RE2 style; no look-around or backreferences) |
| `excludePaths` | string[] | — | Pathname regex patterns to exclude |
| `regexOnFullURL` | boolean | `false` | Match path patterns against full URL including query params |
| `crawlEntireDomain` | boolean | `false` | Follow sibling and parent paths, not just child paths |
| `allowSubdomains` | boolean | `false` | Follow links to subdomains |
| `allowExternalLinks` | boolean | `false` | Follow links off-domain (one hop only; external homepages are skipped) |
| `sitemap` | string | `"include"` | `"include"` (sitemap + HTML links), `"skip"` (HTML links only), `"only"` (sitemap + start URL, no HTML discovery) |
| `ignoreQueryParameters` | boolean | `false` | Avoid re-scraping same path with different query params |
| `ignoreRobotsTxt` | boolean | `false` | Ignore robots.txt — **Enterprise only** |
| `robotsUserAgent` | string | — | Custom User-Agent for robots.txt evaluation — **Enterprise only** |
| `delay` | number | — | Seconds between scrapes; forces concurrency to 1 |
| `maxConcurrency` | integer | — | Max concurrent scrapes; defaults to plan limit |
| `scrapeOptions` | object | — | Per-page scrape options |
| `webhook` | object | — | Webhook config |
| `prompt` | string | — | Natural language to generate crawl options; explicit params override |

### Credit costs (crawl) [3]

- 1 credit per page crawled.
- JSON mode: +4 credits/page.
- PDF parsing: +1 credit/PDF page.

### Job results and expiry [3]

Results are available via the API for **24 hours** after completion. After that, view crawl history in [activity logs](https://www.firecrawl.dev/app/logs). The `data` array contains only successfully scraped pages (even if the target returned a 4xx). Pages Firecrawl failed to scrape (network errors, timeouts, robots.txt blocks) are in `GET /v2/crawl/{id}/errors`, which returns `errors` and `robotsBlocked` arrays [4].

`completed == total` on a finished crawl does **not** guarantee all pages succeeded: `total` excludes failed pages, so the counters converge regardless of failures [4].

### Checking status [3]

Poll `GET /v2/crawl/{id}`. Responses are paginated at 10MB via a `next` URL. `next` is also emitted on non-`completed` statuses — do not use its absence as the exit condition. Terminal condition is `status` being one of `completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled` [4].

### Real-time monitoring [3]

- **WebSocket/watcher**: `firecrawl.watcher(id, { kind: 'crawl', pollInterval, timeout })` — emits `document`, `error`, and `done` events as pages arrive.
- **Webhooks**: configure via the `webhook` parameter with `url`, `metadata`, and `events`. Event types:

| Event | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `crawl.started` | Crawl begins |
| `crawl.page` | Each page successfully scraped |
| `crawl.completed` | Crawl finishes |
| `crawl.failed` | Crawl encounters an error |

Webhook requests include an `X-Firecrawl-Signature` header (HMAC-SHA256). Verify by computing HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with your webhook secret (from account settings → Advanced tab) and comparing with the header value using a timing-safe function [3].

### Key crawl behaviours [3]

- By default, crawl ignores sublinks that are not children of the provided URL. Use `crawlEntireDomain` for sibling/parent paths, `allowSubdomains` for subdomains.
- `sitemap: "include"` (default) uses the sitemap to discover URLs. `"skip"` finds only pages reachable through HTML links — PDFs and deeply nested sitemap-only pages are missed.
- `allowExternalLinks: true` follows off-domain links one hop. Links to an external site's homepage (root URL, no path) are intentionally skipped and reported in Get Crawl Errors with code `EXTERNAL_LINK`.
- Results are non-deterministic between runs: pages are scraped concurrently, and link-discovery order depends on network timing. For more reproducible runs, set `maxConcurrency: 1` or use `sitemap: "only"`.

---

## /map — Fast URL discovery

`POST /v2/map` returns most URLs present on a website without scraping them. URLs come primarily from the site's sitemap, supplemented by SERP results and previously crawled pages [5].

**Cost**: 1 credit per call, regardless of the number of URLs returned (even with `limit: 100000`) [5].

### Usage [5]

```json
{
  "url": "https://firecrawl.dev",
  "limit": 50,
  "sitemap": "include"
}
```

Response returns a `links` array of objects with `url`, `title`, and `description` (title/description not always present) [5].

### Search filtering [5]

Pass `search` to filter for specific URLs inside the site. Response is ordered from most to least relevant.

### Location/language [5]

Same `location` object as `/scrape`: `country` (ISO 3166-1 alpha-2, defaults to `'US'`) and `languages` array.

### Limitations [5]

`/map` prioritises speed over completeness. It may not capture all links — it does not perform recursive HTML-link traversal. For thorough, auditable discovery with error records, use `/crawl`. For links on a single specific page, request the `links` format from `/scrape`.

\
To make requests faster, Firecrawl serves results from cache by default when a recent copy is available.\

- **Default freshness window**: `maxAge = 172800000` ms (2 days). If a cached page is newer than this, it’s returned instantly; otherwise, the page is scraped and then cached.\

The response varies based on the crawl’s status. For incomplete or large responses exceeding 10MB, a `next` URL parameter is provided. You must request this URL to retrieve the next 10MB of data. If the `next` parameter is absent, it indicates the end of the crawl data.

The `skip` and `next` parameters are only relevant when hitting the API directly.
If you’re using the SDK, pagination is handled automatically and all
results are returned at once.

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#real-time-results-with-websocket)  Real-time results with WebSocket\
\
The watcher method provides real-time updates as pages are crawled. Start a crawl, then subscribe to events for immediate data processing.\

Python\
\
Node\

```\
import asyncio\
from firecrawl import AsyncFirecrawl\
\
async def main():\
    firecrawl = AsyncFirecrawl(api_key="fc-YOUR-API-KEY")\
\
    # Start a crawl first\
    started = await firecrawl.start_crawl("https://firecrawl.dev", limit=5)\
\
    # Watch updates (snapshots) until terminal status\
    async for snapshot in firecrawl.watcher(started.id, kind="crawl", poll_interval=2, timeout=120):\
        if snapshot.status == "completed":\
            print("DONE", snapshot.status)\
            for doc in snapshot.data:\
                print("DOC", doc.metadata.source_url if doc.metadata else None)\
        elif snapshot.status == "failed":\
            print("ERR", snapshot.status)\
        else:\
            print("STATUS", snapshot.status, snapshot.completed, "/", snapshot.total)\
\
asyncio.run(main())\
```\

import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl';\
\
const firecrawl = new Firecrawl({ apiKey: 'fc-YOUR-API-KEY' });\

// Start a crawl and then watch it\
const { id } = await firecrawl.startCrawl('https://mendable.ai', {\
  excludePaths: ['blog/*'],\
  limit: 5,\
});\
\
const watcher = firecrawl.watcher(id, { kind: 'crawl', pollInterval: 2, timeout: 120 });\
\
watcher.on('document', (doc) => {\
  console.log('DOC', doc);\
});\
\
watcher.on('error', (err) => {\
  console.error('ERR', err?.error || err);\
});\

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#important-details)  Important details\
\
By default, crawl ignores sublinks that are not children of the URL you provide. For example, `website.com/other-parent/blog-1` would not be returned if you crawled `website.com/blogs/`. Use the `crawlEntireDomain` parameter to include sibling and parent paths. To crawl subdomains like `blog.website.com` when crawling `website.com`, use the `allowSubdomains` parameter.\
\
- **Sitemap discovery**: By default, the crawler includes the website’s sitemap to discover URLs (`sitemap: "include"`). If you set `sitemap: "skip"`, only pages reachable through HTML links from the root URL are found. Assets like PDFs or deeply nested pages listed in the sitemap but not directly linked from HTML will be missed. For maximum coverage, keep the default setting.\
- **Credit usage**: Each page crawled costs 1 credit. JSON mode adds 4 credits per page, and PDF parsing costs 1 credit per PDF page.\
- **Result expiration**: Job results are available via the API for 24 hours after completion. After that, view results in the [activity logs](https://www.firecrawl.dev/app/logs).\
- **Crawl errors**: The `data` array contains pages Firecrawl successfully scraped. Use the [Get Crawl Errors](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/crawl-get-errors) endpoint to retrieve pages that failed due to network errors, timeouts, or robots.txt blocks.\
- **External links**: With `allowExternalLinks: true`, the crawler follows links pointing off your domain and scrapes each linked page once — it does not then crawl the links found on those external pages. Links to an external site’s **homepage** (a root URL with no path, e.g. `https://example.com/`) are intentionally skipped to avoid pulling in an entire unrelated site; these appear in [Get Crawl Errors](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/crawl-get-errors) with the code `EXTERNAL_LINK`. Redirects are followed to their destination — including a link that resolves to its canonical URL (for example `http → https` or the `www` variant) — so only redirects that land on an external homepage are skipped.\
- **Non-deterministic results**: Crawl results may vary between runs of the same configuration, because pages are scraped concurrently and link-discovery order depends on network timing. See [Execution and result accounting](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#execution-and-result-accounting) for what varies and how to make a run more reproducible.\
\
> Are you an AI agent that needs a Firecrawl API key? See [firecrawl.dev/agent-onboarding/SKILL.md](https://www.firecrawl.dev/agent-onboarding/SKILL.md) for automated onboarding instructions.\
\

> From Crawl | Firecrawl › Then check status later\ › [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#execution-and-result-accounting)  Execution and result accounting\ › [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#paging-through-results)  Paging through results\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#paging-through-results)  Paging through results\
\
Responses are capped at 10MB. When a response is truncated, `next` carries the URL for the following page of results.`next` is not purely a “more data remains” signal: it is also emitted whenever `status` is not `completed`, so a terminal `failed` or `cancelled` crawl can return a `next` URL even though no further results exist. Do not use the absence of `next` as your loop’s exit condition — on a failed or cancelled crawl it never disappears.The terminal condition is the status field. To read a run to the end:\
\
1. Poll `GET /v2/crawl/{id}` until `status` is one of `completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled`.\
2. While `next` is present **and** the last page returned a non-empty `data` array, follow `next` to collect the remaining results.\
3. Stop when `next` is absent, or when a page returns no new documents.\
\
The official SDKs handle this paging for you and return all results at once.\
\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#failed-and-blocked-pages)  Failed and blocked pages\
\
[Get Crawl Errors](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/crawl-get-errors) (`GET /v2/crawl/{id}/errors`) records pages that did not make it into `data`. It returns two arrays:\
\
- `errors` — errored scrape jobs, each with `id`, `url`, `error` (the error message), and a `timestamp` of the failure. These are pages Firecrawl itself failed to scrape: network errors, timeouts, and similar. Links to an external site’s homepage that were intentionally skipped are reported here with an error code of `EXTERNAL_LINK`.\
- `robotsBlocked` — URLs that were attempted but blocked by the site’s robots.txt.\
\
This list is not guaranteed to be a complete enumeration of every failure: some internal failure classes are currently filtered out of `errors` before the response is built. Treat it as the record of failures Firecrawl reports, not as a proof that nothing else went wrong. The error code referenced above (`EXTERNAL_LINK`) is returned on error objects today but is not yet part of the published `GET /crawl/{id}/errors` schema; it is pending an API reference update.\
\
A page where the target site returned an HTTP error such as 404 is _not_ a crawl error: Firecrawl scraped it successfully, so it appears in `data` with the site’s status code in `metadata.statusCode`.\
\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#what-the-crawler-is-scoped-to-reach)  What the crawler is scoped to reach\
\
Coverage is bounded by the scope parameters you set, all documented in the [configuration reference](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#configuration-reference) and the [Crawl endpoint reference](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/crawl-post):\
\
- **Children only by default.** Crawl ignores sublinks that are not children of the URL you provide. Use `crawlEntireDomain` for sibling and parent paths, `allowSubdomains` for subdomains, and `allowExternalLinks` to follow links off the domain.\
- **`includePaths` / `excludePaths` match the URL pathname**, as regex patterns — not the full URL, and not query parameters. Set `regexOnFullURL: true` to match against the full URL including query strings instead. The starting URL is also checked against `includePaths`: if it does not match, the crawl may return 0 pages.\
- **Path patterns are Rust regex (RE2-style) and are validated up front.** Look-around and backreferences are not supported, and a pattern that does not compile is rejected with a `400` instead of being silently ignored. Each field accepts at most 1000 patterns of at most 2000 characters each, and `includePaths` and `excludePaths` together may contain at most 1000 patterns and 100,000 characters. For keyword-style filtering, send one short pattern per term (`["pricing", "docs", "blog"]`) rather than combining terms into one long alternation.\
- **Sitemap mode.** With the default `sitemap: "include"`, URLs come from the sitemap plus recursive link discovery. `"skip"` uses HTML links only, so sitemap-only pages such as PDFs or deeply nested pages are missed. `"only"` crawls the sitemap plus the start URL and does not discover links from HTML.\
- **`maxDiscoveryDepth`** caps how many link-discovery hops from the root are followed. Pages at the maximum depth are still scraped, but links found on them are not followed.\
- **`limit`** caps the number of pages, and defaults to `10000`.\
- **`ignoreQueryParameters`** avoids re-scraping the same path with different query parameters.\
- **robots.txt is respected** unless `ignoreRobotsTxt` is enabled (Enterprise only).\
\
`maxConcurrency` defaults to your team’s concurrency limit, which is set by your plan — see [Rate limits](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/rate-limits).\
\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#when-results-vary-between-runs)  When results vary between runs\
\
Crawl results may vary between runs of the same configuration. Pages are scraped concurrently, so the order in which links are discovered depends on network timing and which pages finish loading first. This means different branches of a site may be explored to different extents near the depth boundary, especially at higher `maxDiscoveryDepth` values.To make a run more reproducible:\
\
- Set `maxConcurrency` to `1`. As the [configuration reference](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#configuration-reference) states, `maxConcurrency` is the “maximum concurrent scrapes” — it caps how many requests are in flight at once. That reduces timing-dependent interleaving, but it does not remove run-to-run variation: sitemap discovery is enqueued outside the cap, nested sitemaps are fetched as independent jobs, and the returned `data` array is ordered by finish time rather than discovery order. Setting `delay` also forces concurrency to 1.\
- Use `sitemap: "only"` if the site has a comprehensive sitemap, so the URL set comes from the sitemap rather than from link discovery.\
\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#knowing-when-a-crawl-is-done)  Knowing when a crawl is done\
\
If you are not polling, the [webhook events](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#event-types) tell you the same thing: `crawl.page` fires for each page successfully scraped, and `crawl.completed` (or `crawl.failed`) fires when the run ends. Job results stay retrievable from the API for 24 hours after completion; after that, view them in the [activity logs](https://www.firecrawl.dev/app/logs).\
\

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#configuration-reference)  Configuration reference\
\
The full set of parameters available when submitting a crawl job:\
\
| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |\
| --- | --- | --- | --- |\
| `url` | `string` | (required) | The starting URL to crawl from |\
| `limit` | `integer` | `10000` | Maximum number of pages to crawl |\
| `maxDiscoveryDepth` | `integer` | (none) | Maximum depth from the root URL based on link-discovery hops, not the number of `/` segments in the URL. Each time a new URL is found on a page, it is assigned a depth one higher than the page it was discovered on. The root site and sitemapped pages have a discovery depth of 0. Pages at the max depth are still scraped, but links on them are not followed. |\
| `includePaths` | `string[]` | (none) | URL pathname regex patterns to include. Only matching paths are crawled. At most 1000 patterns of 2000 characters each; see [scope](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#what-the-crawler-is-scoped-to-reach) for the combined limit and regex syntax. |\
| `excludePaths` | `string[]` | (none) | URL pathname regex patterns to exclude from the crawl. Same limits as `includePaths`. |\
| `regexOnFullURL` | `boolean` | `false` | Match `includePaths`/`excludePaths` against the full URL (including query parameters) instead of just the pathname |\
| `crawlEntireDomain` | `boolean` | `false` | Follow internal links to sibling or parent URLs, not just child paths |\
| `allowSubdomains` | `boolean` | `false` | Follow links to subdomains of the main domain |\
| `allowExternalLinks` | `boolean` | `false` | Follow links to external websites. External links are followed one hop (their own links are not crawled), and links pointing to an external site’s homepage are skipped — see [External links](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#external-links). |\
| `sitemap` | `string` | `"include"` | Sitemap handling: `"include"` (default), `"skip"`, or `"only"` |\
| `ignoreQueryParameters` | `boolean` | `false` | Avoid re-scraping the same path with different query parameters |\
| `ignoreRobotsTxt` | `boolean` | `false` | Ignore the website’s robots.txt rules. **Enterprise only** — contact [support@firecrawl.com](mailto:support@firecrawl.com) to enable. |\
| `robotsUserAgent` | `string` | (none) | Custom User-Agent string for robots.txt evaluation. When set, robots.txt is fetched with this User-Agent and rules are matched against it instead of the default. **Enterprise only** — contact [support@firecrawl.com](mailto:support@firecrawl.com) to enable. |\
| `delay` | `number` | (none) | Delay in seconds between scrapes to respect rate limits. Setting this forces concurrency to 1. |\
| `maxConcurrency` | `integer` | (none) | Maximum concurrent scrapes. Defaults to your team’s concurrency limit. |\
| `scrapeOptions` | `object` | (none) | Options applied to every scraped page (formats, proxy, caching, actions, etc.) |\
| `webhook` | `object` | (none) | Webhook configuration for real-time notifications |\
| `prompt` | `string` | (none) | Natural language prompt to generate crawl options. Explicitly set parameters override generated equivalents. |\
\

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#introducing-/map)  Introducing /map

The easiest way to go from a single url to a map of the entire website. This is extremely useful for:

- When you need to prompt the end-user to choose which links to scrape
- Need to quickly know the links on a website
- Need to scrape pages of a website that are related to a specific topic (use the `search` parameter)
- Only need to scrape specific pages of a website

[**Try it in the Playground** \\
\\
Test mapping in the interactive playground — no code required.](https://www.firecrawl.dev/playground?endpoint=map)

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#mapping)  Mapping

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#/map-endpoint)  /map endpoint

Used to map a URL and get urls of the website. This returns most links present on the website.URLs are primarily discovered from the website’s sitemap, supplemented with SERP (search engine) results and previously crawled pages to improve coverage. You can control sitemap behavior with the `sitemap` parameter.

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#installation)  Installation

Python

Node

from firecrawl import Firecrawl

  # No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:

)
```

```
// npm install firecrawl

import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl';

const firecrawl = new Firecrawl({
  // No API key needed to get started — add one for higher rate limits:

```

# Authenticate (one-time setup)

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#usage)  Usage

Python

Node

cURL

CLI

```
from firecrawl import Firecrawl

firecrawl = Firecrawl(api_key="fc-YOUR-API-KEY")
res = firecrawl.map(url="https://firecrawl.dev", limit=50, sitemap="include")
print(res)
```

```
import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl';

const firecrawl = new Firecrawl({ apiKey: "fc-YOUR-API-KEY" });

const res = await firecrawl.map('https://firecrawl.dev', { limit: 50, sitemap: 'include' });
console.log(res);
```

    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \

      "url": "https://firecrawl.dev"

```

```
# Map a website to discover URLs
firecrawl map https://firecrawl.dev

# Output as JSON with limit
firecrawl map https://firecrawl.dev --json --limit 100 --pretty
```

Each map request consumes 1 credit per call, regardless of the number of URLs returned. For example, setting `limit` to 100,000 still uses 1 credit.

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#response)  Response

SDKs will return the data object directly. cURL will return the payload exactly as shown below.

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#location-and-language)  Location and Language

Specify country and preferred languages to get relevant content based on your target location and language preferences, similar to the scrape endpoint.

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#how-it-works)  How it works

When you specify the location settings, Firecrawl will use an appropriate proxy if available and emulate the corresponding language and timezone settings. By default, the location is set to ‘US’ if not specified.

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#usage-2)  Usage

To use the location and language settings, include the `location` object in your request body with the following properties:

- `country`: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code (e.g., ‘US’, ‘AU’, ‘DE’, ‘JP’). Defaults to ‘US’.
- `languages`: An array of preferred languages and locales for the request in order of priority. Defaults to the language of the specified location.

Python

Node

cURL

```
from firecrawl import Firecrawl

firecrawl = Firecrawl(api_key="fc-YOUR-API-KEY")

res = firecrawl.map('https://example.com',
    location={
        'country': 'US',
        'languages': ['en']
    }
)

print(res)
```

```
import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl';

const firecrawl = new Firecrawl({ apiKey: "fc-YOUR-API-KEY" });

const res = await firecrawl.map('https://example.com', {
  location: { country: 'US', languages: ['en'] },
});

console.log(res.metadata);
```

```
curl -X POST "https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/map" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FIRECRAWL_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "url": "https://example.com",
    "location": { "country": "US", "languages": ["en"] }
  }'
```

For more details about supported locations, refer to the [Proxies documentation](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/proxies).

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#considerations)  Considerations

This endpoint prioritizes speed, so it may not capture all website links. It primarily relies on the website’s sitemap, supplemented by cached crawl data and search engine results. For a more thorough and up-to-date list of URLs, consider using the [/crawl](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl) endpoint instead.If you need more thorough recursive discovery with auditable result and error records rather than a fast approximation, use [/crawl](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl), which discovers pages by recursive link traversal as well as the sitemap and reports what it returned and what it failed to fetch — see [Execution and result accounting](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#execution-and-result-accounting). For the links on one specific page, request the [`links` format](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/scrape#scrape-formats) from [/scrape](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/scrape).

> Are you an AI agent that needs a Firecrawl API key? See [firecrawl.dev/agent-onboarding/SKILL.md](https://www.firecrawl.dev/agent-onboarding/SKILL.md) for automated onboarding instructions.
